reflection_text.6:
The riddle is a charade built on *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* and *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *quodque fit ex illis … fur dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Syntactic frame. *sequatur* is 3sg subjunctive. In the first hemistich the subject is *Didonis prima* nom. fem. and the accusative object is *Penelopes primam*. So *Didonis prima sequitur Penelopes primam*: “Dido’s first follows Penelope’s first”. Object precedes subject in the wording, subject follows object in execution. The second hemistich is the same construction with *sequatur* elided: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. and *primam Cadmi* acc., i.e. *syllaba prima Remi sequitur primam Cadmi*: “Remus’s first syllable follows Cadmus’s first”. So the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses is Penelope → Dido and Cadmus → Remus.

Segmentation dispute. 
* Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp: *primam* = first syllable for all four names, *syllaba prima* is just explicit emphasis for Remus. With the *sequatur* order Penelope→Dido→Cadmus→Remus this gives Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare / pendicare*. *pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks, manacle; *pedicare* = to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet. The thief *deprensus in horto* will have to give / undergo that, i.e. be fettered/put in the stocks. Later vulgar gloss adds the obscene sexual sense of *pedicare*. Supporters in round 1: 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8. Round 0 majority was on this reading.

* Deprecare camp: *primam* is first letter, not first syllable, and the poet marks the syllable explicitly only for Remus: *syllaba prima Remi*. Hence Penelope = P, Dido = D, Cadmus = C, Remus = Re-. With the *sequatur* order the blocks compose as Dido follows Penelope = P then D, and Remus follows Cadmus = C? Wait subject follows object, so Cadmus first then Remus: Re + C if the construction is read as object→subject in the linear string. The linear composition promoted by 1,13,14,5,7,9 is D P Re C = depreca-, *deprecare/deprecari* “to entreat, beg pardon, give preces”. The *deprensus* ~ *deprecare* pun is taken as the riddle’s point, and the penalty is supplication/prayer for pardon, something the *fur* can *dare*.

Cruxes noted in round 1. Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, so Pe-Di-Ca-Re forces a truncation *Pe-*; *pendicare* Pen-Di-Ca-Re is the form several colleagues cite, 5,7,13. The *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction is used to argue for a letter/syllable mix, which makes the Pe-Di-Ca-Re segmentation unstable. The order reversal in the second hemistich is contested: *sequatur* puts *syllaba prima Remi* after *primam Cadmi* i.e. Ca-Re under the Pe-Di-Ca-Re parse, but the grammatical reading of subject follows object gives Re-C in the linear string, i.e. D P Re C.

Current state. The syntactic parse is solid: subject follows object, giving Penelope before Dido and Cadmus before Remus. Whether *primam* means first syllable or first letter remains the fork. The traditional school gloss is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* = pedica, fetter/stocks, with the vulgar extension noted. The deprecare reading respects the *primam/syllaba prima* distinction and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo, and is argued as grammatically more consistent by 1,13,14,5,7,9. Colleague 2 explicitly acknowledges both parses and notes the ordinary tradition takes Pe-Di-Ca-Re. Unresolved is whether the riddle intends the literal legal punishment of fettering or the *deprecare* supplication, and whether the vulgar sexual sense is a later gloss or the intended pun.
reflection_text.12:
The charade is built around Penelope / Dido / Cadmus / Remus and the instruction *sequatur*. The two camps remain Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pendicare vs. D-P-Re-C = deprecare/deprecari.

For pedicare / fettering:
* Colleagues 2,4,6,10,11,12,14,8 read the verse in verse order as Pe- Di- Ca- Re- = pedicare, pedica f. foot-fetter, stocks, to fetter/put in the stocks. 10,4,6,8 explicitly treat *sequatur* as understood as “let X follow Y” in the order the names are mentioned: Pe- is followed by Di-, Ca- is followed by Re-. The threatened *poena* is therefore to be pedicated, i.e. to be fettered/put in stocks, vulgarly glossed as the obscene *pedicare*. 11 and 12 add the later vulgar sexual gloss; 13 notes the Pen- vs Pe- instability – Penelopes primam is naturally Pen- giving Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare.
* 3 and 4 keep the object-subject order *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* but still map it to Pe-Di- and *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* to Ca-Re-, arriving at Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

For deprecare / supplication:
* Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 argue *sequatur* is syntactically decisive. *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* is subject Didonis prima, object Penelopes primam: “let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first”, i.e. the block is D + P. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = “let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first”, i.e. Re + C. With *primam* taken as first letter and *syllaba prima Remi* explicitly marked as a syllable, the four pieces in the order commanded by the two *sequatur* clauses are D P Re C → depreca-.
* The pun *deprensus in horto* ~ *deprecare* is repeatedly cited as rhetorically fitting: the caught thief is condemned to give *preces*, to deprecate/beg pardon. 1,7,13 stress the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction: the poet says *syllaba prima* only for Remus, suggesting *primam* elsewhere means first letter, not first syllable. 14 and 7 note the Pe- vs Pen- problem: Penelope’s first syllable is Pen-, not Pe-, so a consistent syllabic reading forces Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, undermining the neat Pe-Di-Ca-Re form. 5,7,13 also note that *dare* wants something offerable, and *deprecare/preces dare* fits better than “give a fetter”.

Unresolved: whether *primam* means first letter or first syllable, and whether *sequatur* is read as “X follows Y in the order of mention” or as a strict grammatical subject-object inversion. The Pe- / Pen- inconsistency remains a weakness for the pedicare camp, while the pedicare camp retains the weight of traditional manuscript glosses and the simple verse-order concatenation.

I am now giving more weight to the syntactic/lexical argument for deprecare/deprecari – supplication, to beg pardon – because of the explicit *syllaba prima* marking, the *sequatur* order D-P, Re-C, and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo. The classical pedicare = fetter/stocks reading, with its vulgar *pedicare* extension, remains the most frequent traditional gloss and cannot be dismissed; it is the reading most colleagues still defend.
reflection_text.11:
The verse is a four-beginning charade. The crux is how *sequatur* and *primam / syllaba prima* are read.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: “let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first”. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* ellipsed: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: “let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first”. 

Pedicare camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,10,11,12 – reads *primam* as “first syllable” throughout, with the explicit marking *syllaba prima Remi* taken as confirmation. In the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses they put
Penelope’s first → Dido’s first → Cadmus’ first → Remus’ first syllable,
i.e. Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re, normally cited as *pedicare/pendicare* < *pedica* f. “foot-fetter, stocks”. *quodque fit ex illis … fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is therefore “you caught in the hortus will give me what is made out of them: with this penalty your guilt is atoned”. Classically *pedicare* = to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet; in the later vulgar tradition the same form is glossed in its obscene sense. The camp notes the Pe- vs Pen- problem – Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-* – and that the *pedicare* gloss is internally split between literal fetter/stocks and vulgar sodomy.

Deprecare camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 – stresses the *primam vs syllaba prima* distinction. Only Remus is explicitly *syllaba prima*; *Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are read as first letter, not syllable. With the *sequatur* order respected the first block is Dido’s first after Penelope’s first = D + P, the second block is Remus’ first syllable after Cadmus’ first = Re + C. In composition order that is *D P Re C* = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* “to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces”. The pun *deprensus in horto* ~ *deprecare* is taken as the riddle’s intended word-play, and the penalty is to give a prayer/supplication, to *deprecari* for mercy. Colleague 1,13,14,7,9 argue that the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation ignores the *sequatur* ordering in the second hemistich – it turns the required Re C into Ca Re – and forces *primam* to mean first syllable where the verse marks syllable only for Remus. Colleague 13,14,5,7 also note that a strict syllable reading would give *Pen-* not *Pe-* and thus *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

Round 0 split is maintained in Round 1, with Colleague 10 moving from a deprecare reading in Round 0 to a pedicare reading in Round 1. Colleague 2 and 3 now explicitly note the formal grammatical reading would give the deprecare anagram *D-Pe-Re-C* but say the ordinary tradition takes the straight verse order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

Unresolved: whether *primam* is systematically first syllable or first letter; whether the first segment is Pe- or Pen-; how strictly the *sequatur* object→subject order is to be mapped onto the charade linear order; and how much weight to give the *deprensus/deprecare* echo versus the traditional *pedicare/pendicare* gloss and its literal fetter vs vulgar sexual divergence. The discussion remains essentially 50/50 between a literal/physical penalty of fettering/stocks – *pedicare* – and a rhetorical penalty of supplication – *deprecare/deprecari* – with the latter gaining strength from the grammatical *primam/syllaba prima* distinction and the *deprensus* pun.
reflection_text.10:
The grammatical core I carried over is the nominative-accusative structure of *sequatur*. *Penelopes primam* is accusative, *Didonis prima* is nominative subject of *sequatur*: *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* = “Dido’s first follows Penelope’s first”. By ellipsis the second hemistich is parallel: *syllaba prima Remi* is nominative, *Cadmi primam* accusative, so *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = “the first syllable of Remus follows the first of Cadmus”. That gives the linear order Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus.

With the usual syllabic reading that is
* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima = Di-
* Cadmi primam = Ca-
* Remi syllaba prima = Re-
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* / *pendicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is the verb built out of the four beginnings. *pedica* f. is the foot-fetter, the stocks, the manica pedis; *pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is therefore “you caught in the garden, thief, will give me what is made out of them: with this penalty your guilt is to be atoned”. Classically the poena is being fettered/put in the stocks; in the later vulgar tradition the same form is the familiar obscene garden-thief gloss.

Round 1 preserves that consensus in Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8. The main competing line is *deprecare/deprecari*. Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9 argue *primam* is a letter-signal and only *Remi* is explicitly *syllaba prima*, and that *sequatur* forces the blocks D P Re C → *depreca-*. The pun *deprensus/deprecare* and the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction are the evidence for that reading.

Against it: treating *primam* as first letter for Penelope/Dido/Cadmus but first syllable for Remus is unstable; *Penelopes primam* as a first syllable is naturally *Pen-* not *Pe-*, which forces *pendicare* in the syllabic camp; the deprecare camp must reverse the second block from Ca-Re to Re-Ca and also invert the first block in the order of composition, i.e. it has to ignore the object-subject order that *sequatur* actually sets for the first hemistich. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is neat, but it comes at the cost of the consistent *primam = first syllable* reading and of the order Penelope→Dido, Cadmus→Remus that *sequatur* gives.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether the intended literal classical penalty is the physical *pedica*, stocks/fettering, or the later vulgar sexual sense of *pedicare*, and whether the deliberate *primam / syllaba prima* wording is a true letter/syllable cue for *deprecare* or a red herring. My current working interpretation stays with the grammatically consistent syllabic charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, i.e. the thief is threatened with being fettered/put in the stocks, the form conventionally cited in the medieval transmission as the garden-thief’s obscene *pedicatio*.
reflection_text.8:
The riddle is a charade on Penelope / Dido / Cadmus / Remus built around *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. The core dispute is segmentation, the meaning of *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima*, and the order imposed by *sequatur*.

The classic scholastic / mass reading is a syllable chain in verse order.

* Penelopes primam = Pe- [some read Pen-], Didonis prima = Di-, so *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* = Di- follows Pe- → Pe-Di-
* primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, with *sequatur* understood as *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = Re- follows Ca- → Ca-Re-
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* / *pendicare*.

*quodque fit ex illis … fur dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is then the thing made out of them. *pedica* is the foot-fetter, stocks, manacle; *pedicare* is to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet. In the later vulgar tradition the same form is glossed in its obscene sexual sense, *pedicatio*. The punishment threatened to the *fur deprensus in horto* is therefore being fettered/put in stocks, commonly rendered as the garden-thief joke.

The main variants inside this camp are Pe- vs Pen- giving *pedicare* vs *pendicare*, and literal fetter/stocks vs vulgar sexual reading.

A substantial minority insists on the strict syntax and the *primam / syllaba prima* marking.

*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* is subject *Didonis prima* + accusative object *Penelopes primam*: “let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first”. The second hemistich is parallel with ellipsis: *syllaba prima Remi* nominative, *primam Cadmi* accusative, so “let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first”. 
The poet marks only Remus with *syllaba prima*; Penelope, Dido, Cadmus are only *primam/prima*, which is taken as the first letter signal, not a syllable. That gives P, D, C and explicit Re-. Keeping the follow-order gives P then D and C then Re, i.e. in composition order D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to make supplication’. The pun *deprensus in horto* / *deprecare* is then the point of the riddle: the caught thief is condemned to give a *deprecatio*, to beg mercy, and *hac poena culpa luenda est* fits a penalty of supplication.

The *deprecare* camp argues the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation ignores the *sequatur* order in the second half – it needs Ca-Re where the grammar gives Re-C – and papers over the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction. The *pedicare* camp replies that *sequatur* is read in the natural verse order Pe followed by Di and Ca followed by Re, and that the usual scholastic gloss is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

Unresolved: whether *primam* means first letter or first syllable and whether Penelope’s first is Pe- or Pen-; whether *sequatur* is to be read as Y then X in the charade or X then Y; whether the intended penalty is the literal stocks/fetter, the vulgar sexual *pedicatio*, or the rhetorical supplication *deprecari*. The deprensus/deprecare echo remains the strongest formal argument for the supplication reading, while the sheer weight of traditional glosses supports *pedicare* as the intended surface solution.
reflection_text.3:
The riddle is a charade built from Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, Remus and the verb sequatur governs the order.

The object-subject-verb reading that I favoured last round is:
Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam, ‘Dido’s first follows Penelope’s first’. With the verb understood in the second hemistich, syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi, ‘Remus’ first syllable follows Cadmus’ first’. In linear order that is Penelope’s first → Dido’s first → Cadmus’ first → Remus’ first syllable.

That yields Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare / pendicare. quodque fit ex illis is the verb made out of them, and quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the threat to the caught garden thief.

Colleagues 10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8 keep this Pe-Di-Ca-Re ordering. Pedica is the foot-fetter, the stocks, manica pedis; pedicare is to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet. That is the classical penal gloss, the ‘pay with the feet’ penalty. Colleague 11 and the vulgar tradition add the later obscene sense of pedicare, and the two senses are the same morphological form.

The alternative, pushed hard in round 1 by Colleagues 1,13,14,5,7,9, is to respect the primam / syllaba prima marking and the sequatur ordering more strictly. They argue primam is used for first letter for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, while only Remus is explicitly syllaba prima. With primam = first letter P, D, C and syllaba prima Remi = Re-, and with the subject following the object, the two sequatur clauses are read as Dido’s first follows Penelope’s first and Cadmus’ first follows Remus’ first syllable, giving D P Re C = D-Pe-Re-C = depreca- / deprecare / deprecari ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. The deprensus in horto / deprecare pun is then the point of the riddle and the poena is supplication / begging pardon.

Arguments for pedicare: sequatur is consistently object then subject, giving Pe then Di and Ca then Re; the verse is the familiar school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare, attested with both the fetter/stocks and the vulgar gloss; the deprecare reading needs to reverse the second block to Re C and to treat primam as letter for three names and syllable for one.

Arguments for deprecare: the poet marks syllaba prima only for Remus, implying primam elsewhere means first letter; Penelopes primam is naturally Pen- not Pe-, which makes Pe-Di-Ca-Re unstable and gives Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare; the deprensus / deprecare echo is a classic riddle pun and the verb dare fits giving preces better than giving a fetter; the sequatur ordering is kept consistently and no Pen- vs Pe- problem arises.

Unresolved: whether primam is to be read uniformly as first syllable/element or as first letter with syllaba prima explicitly marked; whether the second hemistich is Ca Re or Re C under sequatur; whether Penelope’s primam is Pe- or Pen-; the exact status of the pedica = fetter vs vulgar pedicatio gloss; and whether the riddle intends the physical pedica penalty or the rhetorical penalty of deprecari. The pedicare reading remains the majority traditional gloss and the one the syntax Pe-Di-Ca-Re supports, but the deprecare reading with its primam/syllaba distinction and deprensus pun is a credible grammatically elegant alternative and accounts for the D-P-Re-C analyses.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The word-play that the riddle is built around is the echo of *deprensus* in the threat *quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is subject–object with the verb *sequatur*. The subject is *Didonis prima*, the accusative object is *Penelopes primam*: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The block is therefore P followed by D, not Pe followed by Di in the order of composition.

The same ellipse is at work in the second hemistich. *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: let Remus’s first syllable follow Cadmus’s first. The block is therefore Re followed by C.

Put together in the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe we have D P Re C, the charade *de-pre-ca-*.

That is why the poet marks only Remus with *syllaba prima*. *Penelopes primam*, *Didonis prima*, *primam Cadmi* are left without *syllaba*; the author is signalling the first letter, not the first syllable. If *primam* were meant as first syllable throughout we would have *Pen-* from Penelope, not *Pe-*, and with the D-P order imposed by *sequatur* the first block would be *Pen-Di-*, i.e. *pendi-*, as 5,7 and 13 already note. That is the classical gloss of the school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*; in the later vulgar transmission the same form is the familiar obscene reading of the garden-thief joke.

The word-play that the riddle is built around is the echo of *deprensus* in the threat *quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is subject–object with the verb *sequatur*. The subject is *Didonis prima*, the accusative object is *Penelopes primam*: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The block is therefore P followed by D, not Pe followed by Di in the order of composition.

The same ellipse is at work in the second hemistich. *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: let Remus’s first syllable follow Cadmus’s first. The block is therefore Re followed by C.

Put together in the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe we have D P Re C, the charade *de-pre-ca-*.

That is why the poet marks only Remus with *syllaba prima*. *Penelopes primam*, *Didonis prima*, *primam Cadmi* are left without *syllaba*; the author is signalling the first letter, not the first syllable. If *primam* were meant as first syllable throughout we would have *Pen-* from Penelope, not *Pe-*, and with the D-P order imposed by *sequatur* the first block would be *Pen-Di-*, i.e. *pendi-*, as 5,7 and 13 already note. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation therefore needs two incompatible adjustments at once: it has to read *primam* as syllable for Penelope and Dido but as letter for Cadmus, and it has to reverse the order that *sequatur* sets for the second pair from Re C to Ca Re.

The *deprecare/deprecari* reading keeps the distinction *primam* vs *syllaba prima* intact and respects the follow-order in both hemistichs. It also gives the riddle its aesthetic payoff: *tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis* — the thief who is *deprensus* is condemned to give a *deprecatio*, to *deprecare* for pardon. *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is exactly the poetic way of saying the guilt is atoned by supplication, something that can be *datum*.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp is also internally unstable. 10 and 3 themselves note that the strict grammatical reading of *sequatur … et …* yields *deprecare/deprecari* and they retreat to “ordinary tradition” for *pedicare*. 11 then glosses that same form with the vulgar sodomy sense of *pedicatio*, while 2,4,6,12 gloss it with the classical *pedica* fetter/stocks. Those are not the same penalty, and the split between *Pe-* vs *Pen-* in the first block shows the segmentation is being stretched to fit a familiar word.

Keeping the order imposed by *sequatur* and the author’s own *primam / syllaba prima* marking gives a clean charade D-P-Re-C, *deprecare*, and the neat *deprensus : deprecare* pun that the *fur* will have to give as his *poena*.

I keep coming back to the way the verse marks what it wants a syllable and what it does not.

When the poet wants a syllable he says it: *syllaba prima Remi*. He does not say *syllaba prima* for Penelope, Dido or Cadmus, he says *primam*...*prima*...*primam*. That is the normal signal for the first letter / first element, and the explicit *syllaba* for Remus is then a deliberate contrast. If *primam* were meant as first syllable everywhere we would have *Pen-* from Penelope, not *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re would already be strained to Pen-Di-Ca-Re.

The syntax is then decisive. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is subject *Didonis prima* with accusative object *Penelopes primam*: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The first block is therefore D after P, D P, not P then D in the order of composition.

The second hemistich is the exact parallel with *sequatur* understood: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. Let Remus’s first syllable follow Cadmus’s first. That is Re after C, i.e. Re C in the order the verse commands.

Put the two blocks together in the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe you get D P Re C, the charade DPeReC.

That is *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. And the riddle rewards the ordering with the pun it is built on: *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief who is *deprensus* is condemned to *deprecare*. You do not *dare* a fetter in the sense the verse uses *dabis* — you *dare preces*, you give supplication. *Hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is exactly the poetic way of saying the guilt is atoned by entreaty.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading has to flatten the primam / syllaba prima distinction and then reverse the second block from Re C to Ca Re in order to get a familiar form. Once the distinction is kept and *sequatur* is kept, the verse gives us the deprensus / deprecare echo and a penalty that is something the caught thief can actually *give*: a prayer for pardon, not a physical fetter whose semantics are also split in the camp between literal *pedica* stocks and the later vulgar sense.

I’ve been going back over the syntax of the two sequatur clauses because that’s where the ordering really lives, and I think it is breaking the straight Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is subject = Didonis prima, accusative = Penelopes primam. It is literally “let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first”. That is a D + P block, not Pe first then Di. The same construction is elided in the second hemistich: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*, i.e. “let Cadmus’ first follow Remus’ first syllable”. That is a Re + C block.

The poet also marks the syllable explicitly only once. He says *syllaba prima Remi*, not *primam Remi*. *Primam* for Penelope, Dido and Cadmus is therefore the normal “first letter” signal, while Remus is given as an explicit syllable Re-. If *primam* really meant “first syllable” everywhere we would have Pen- from Penelope, not Pe-, and Pe-Di-Ca-Re would become Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare, the problem 5,7,13 already flagged. The Pe- truncation is an artificial fix to rescue pedicare.

Put the blocks together in the order sequatur prescribes: D P Re C. That is the charade DPeReC, deprecare/deprecari. It also gives the riddle the word-play it is built on: *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis* – the thief who is deprensus is told to *dare* what is made of those pieces, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. Deprensus : deprecare is exactly the kind of echo a Latin charade loves, and *dare* a fetter is awkward, whereas *dare preces, deprecare* is something you can be made to give.

On the pedicare reading there is also the internal split that worries me. 11 reads the result as the vulgar sexual sense, 12/2/4/6/10 read it as *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. Those are not the same poena, and the need to keep both shows the segmentation is being stretched. Once primam vs syllaba prima and the sequatur order are kept, the order Re C rather than Ca Re falls out naturally, and the penalty becomes the supplication the caught gardener has to perform.

The charade is Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is the normal *A sequitur B* construction: the subject is *Didonis prima*, the accusative object is *Penelopes primam*. “Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.”  In the usual scholastic syllabic reading

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima = Di-

and the *sequatur* gives Pe- + Di- = Pe-Di-.

The second hemistich is the same construction with the verb elided:

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*.  
*primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, and the verb again gives Ca- + Re- = Ca-Re-.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re is what *quodque fit ex illis* is.

*pedica* f. is the foot-fetter, the manica pedis, the stocks. *pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in the stocks.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is therefore:

you who are caught in the hortus, thief, will give me what is made out of them: with this penalty your guilt is to be atoned.

The *poena* threatened to the *fur deprensus in horto* is to be pedicated, to be put in the pedica/fetters/stocks, i.e. to pay with the feet. That is the classical school gloss *pedicare*, regularly cited in the later vulgar transmission in its familiar obscene sense *pedicatio*.

The charade is controlled by *sequatur* and by the way the verse marks letter against syllable.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is subject – object: *Didonis prima ... sequatur Penelopes primam*. Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The first block in the order the verb prescribes is therefore D followed by P. 

The second hemistich is the exact parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. Let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. The second block in the order the verb prescribes is therefore Re followed by C.

The poet is careful with his notation. He says *syllaba prima* only once, for Remus, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. *primam* / *prima* elsewhere is used for the first letter, P, D, C. Taken in the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses we get

D P + Re C = D P R E C

*depreca-* , *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* then makes the pun the riddle is built on. The *fur* who is *deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis* what is made out of the pieces, and the penalty with which his *culpa* is to be *luenda* is precisely the *deprecat io* that echoes *deprensus*. He will have to give preces, he will be condemned to supplication, to beg pardon for the theft.

That is the reading that respects *sequatur* and the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction. The familiar school gloss Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, *pedica* f. foot-fetter, stocks, and in later vulgar usage the obscene extension, is the verse-order concatenation that ignores the subject-object order of *sequatur* and the Re-C order forced by the second hemistich, and it requires Penelope’s first syllable to be read as Pe- instead of Pen-. It is the traditional citation of the riddle, but grammatically it is the verse-order reading, not the reading the syntax commands.

On a strict grammatical/syntactic construal the poena the verse names is the obligation to *deprecare*, to make supplication and beg pardon.
public_text.13:
The marking *syllaba prima* vs *primam/prima* is doing real work here and I think it decides the order.

The poet only says *syllaba prima* once, with Remus. Penelope, Dido and Cadmus are all given *primam/prima*. In Latin charades *prima* without *syllaba* is the normal signal for the first letter, not the first syllable. If he had wanted a syllable for Penelope he would have written *syllaba prima Penelopes* just as he does for Remus. Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, which is why the *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* camp keeps having to slide between *pedicare* and *pendicare*.

*sequatur* is then parallel in both hemistichs. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is acc. + nom. + subjunctive: *Didonis prima* is the subject, *Penelopes primam* the object. Literally ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. That is P followed by D in the order the verb requires.

The second half is the same construction with the verb elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi* is made to follow *primam Cadmi*. It is Re followed by C.

Put the two blocks together in the order *sequatur* prescribes: D P Re C.

That is *depreca-*, *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to make supplication’. It is the only reading that keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction intact and respects the follow-order in both hemistichs.

It also gives the riddle its internal pun. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief is *deprensus in horto*: the caught thief is condemned to *deprecare*, to give a *deprecatio*. You can *dare preces*; it is a thing you can give. A fetter is something you suffer, not something you *dabis* in the sense the verse uses.

The *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* = *pedicare* reading has to reverse the order imposed by *sequatur* in the second hemistich, turn Re C into Ca Re, and it leaves the camp split between *pedica* ‘stocks/fetter’ and the later vulgar gloss. The instability is a sign the segmentation is being stretched to a familiar word. *deprecare* keeps the grammar, keeps the letter/syllable marking, and explains the *deprensus / deprecare* echo that the riddle is built on. That is the poena the verse names.
public_text.14:
The sequatur clauses have to be taken syntactically and the marking of *syllaba* has to be taken literally, otherwise the poem is creating a problem for itself.

*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* is *Didonis prima* nom. + *Penelopes primam* acc. : let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The subject comes first in the sentence-order, the object is what is followed. The two pieces are therefore to be placed in the order Penelope → Dido, but the verb tells us the piece that follows is the subject, so the block is read as D following P. The same construction is elided in the second hemistich.

The poet is careful with terminology. He marks Remus explicitly as *syllaba prima Remi*. He does not mark Penelope, Dido or Cadmus with *syllaba*. *Primam / prima / primam* is therefore not being used here for ‘first syllable’. It is the first element, the first letter. That is why we get a mismatch if we force a syllable reading everywhere: *Penelopes primam* would then want *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re segmentation collapses into *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*. The text avoids that by reserving *syllaba prima* for the one case where a syllable really is required.

With that distinction kept, the four elements are P, D, C and Re-. In the order the two *sequatur* clauses impose we have

*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → P then D
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* → C then Re, i.e. *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re follows C

That is P D Re C in the order of composition, D P Re C when the verb is read in its natural subject-object direction: de-pre-ca-.

*Quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *deprecare/deprecari*, ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. And the echo is in the verse itself: *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief who is *deprensus* is condemned to give the thing made out of the pieces, and you give *deprecare* by *dare*: *preces dare, deprecari*. The penalty is a supplication, a prayer for pardon, exactly the kind of word-play a riddle about being caught in the garden wants.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation requires ignoring the explicit *syllaba* marking, reversing the second *sequatur* to Ca-Re instead of Re-C, and then smoothing over the Pen- vs Pe- inconsistency. Once *primam* is kept as first letter and *sequatur* is kept as the ordering verb, the charade is depreca-, and the poena is the *deprecatio* the fur must give.
public_text.9:
The distinction the poet makes between primam and syllaba prima is not decorative.

Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are all given without syllaba. Only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima. That is the normal Latin way of signalling ‘first letter/element’ with primam/prima and ‘first syllable’ with syllaba prima. If the poet wanted Pe- from Penelope he would have marked it syllaba prima, as he does for Remus; Penelopes primam is P, not Pe-, and the same goes for the prima of Dido and the primam of Cadmus. The only syllable we are actually licensed to take is Re- from Remus.

The syntax then fixes the order. Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The two elements are therefore given in the order in which the verse names them, Dido then Penelope, and the second hemistich is the exact parallel with sequatur understood: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi, let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. That is Remus then Cadmus.

We therefore have in the order the two sequatur-clauses prescribe: D P for the first pair and Re C for the second pair. Put together D P Re C = depreca-. quodque fit ex illis is deprecare / deprecari, ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’.

That is not a forced reading. The line then punishes the fur deprensus in horto with precisely the thing he can dare: mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis quodque fit ex illis. You caught in the garden will give me what is made out of those pieces. You give a deprecatio, you are condemned to deprecari, to make supplication for mercy. hac poena culpa luenda tua est fits exactly: the guilt is atoned by a prayer of entreaty.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation has to ignore the primam / syllaba prima asymmetry and it has to reverse the order that sequatur sets up in the second hemistich in order to get Ca before Re. It also has to make Penelopes primam = Pe- when Penelope’s first syllable is Pen-, which is why the camp keeps slipping to pendicare. Once primam is read consistently as first letter and sequatur is read consistently in both hemistichs, the elegant deprensus : deprecare echo is preserved and the penalty is the supplication the thief must give, not a physical fetter.

The verse is a straight sequitur-charade and the order is fixed by the two *sequatur* clauses.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequitur Penelopes primam*. Nominative *Didonis prima* follows accusative *Penelopes primam*. The block is therefore Penelope’s first followed by Dido’s first.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is the same construction with *sequatur* understood. In the verse the accusative *primam Cadmi* precedes the nominative *syllaba prima Remi*, i.e. *syllaba prima Remi sequitur primam Cadmi*. The block is therefore Cadmus’ first followed by Remus’ first syllable.

On the usual school reading *primam/prima* is ‘first syllable’ and *syllaba prima* is the explicit marking of the same for Remus. That gives

Penelopes primam = Pe-
Didonis prima   = Di-
primam Cadmi     = Ca-
Remi syllaba prima = Re-

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedica-re*, *quodque fit ex illis*.

*pedica* f. is the foot-fetter, the stocks, the manica pedum. *pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in the stocks. The speaker says

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

the thing made out of them you, thief caught in the hortus, will give me; with this poena your culpa is to be atoned.

Classically the poena threatened to the *fur deprensus in horto* is therefore the *pedica*: to be pedicated, to be fettered/put in the stocks. That is the ordinary school gloss *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare*, which in the later vulgar transmission of the hortus joke is the familiar *pedicatio* sense. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is attractive, but it requires reversing the sequatur order in the second hemistich to Re-C and treating *primam* as first letter everywhere while keeping *syllaba prima* as syllable, and it destroys the regular *primam/prima = first syllable* charade that the verse is built on.

The two hemistichs are parallel charades built on sequitur/se-quatur.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is nominative + accusative: 
Didonis prima nom. sequitur Penelopes primam acc. = ‘let Dido’s first
follow Penelope’s first’. The composition is therefore Penelope’s first
and then Dido’s first.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is the same construction with
sequatur understood: syllaba prima Remi nom. sequitur primam Cadmi acc.
= ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The composition is
therefore Cadmus’ first and then Remus’ first syllable.

In Latin syllabification

Pe-ne-lo-pe, Di-do-nis, Ca-dmi, Re-mi

Penelope’s first syllable is Pe-, Dido’s first syllable is Di-, Cadmus’
first syllable is Ca-, Remus’ first syllable is Re-. 
Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

*quodque fit ex illis … fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is
the charade formula: ‘what is made out of them you, thief caught in the

What is made out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re is

*pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manacle for the feet’

*pedicare* ‘to put in the pedica, to fetter, to shackle the feet, to put
in the stocks’.

That is the thing the deprensus in horto is told he will *dare* and the
poena with which his culpa is to be luenda.  Classically it is the
literal penal action of being fettered/put in the stocks; in the later
vulgar transmission of the school riddle the same form is the familiar
vulgar gloss of the garden-thief joke. The deprensus/deprecare echo is
a later rhetorical embellishment. The verse as written commands the
order Pe-Di, Ca-Re and the syllabic segmentation that the text itself
gives, i.e. pedicare/pendicare.

The two sequatur clauses are the jigsaw.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam.  
Didonis prima is nom. sg. fem., Penelopes primam acc. sg. fem. ‘Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’.

et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi.  
syllaba prima Remi is nom. sg. fem., primam Cadmi acc. sg. fem. ‘Let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’.

In the linear order imposed by the two followings we therefore have

Penelope’s first → Dido’s first → Cadmus’ first → Remus’ first syllable

Pe-  Di-  Ca-  Re-

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = quodque fit ex illis. 

quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est.

The thing made out of the four beginnings is pedica-re. pedica f. is the foot-fetter, the stocks, the manica pedis. pedicare is pedicae dare, to put in the pedica, to fetter / shackle the feet, to put in the stocks. That is the concrete penal action which the speaker threatens to the fur deprensus in horto: you who are caught in the garden will have to give / undergo what is made out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re, and with that poena your culpa is to be luenda.

The charade is built on the two sequatur clauses exactly as they are written. 

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: Dido’s first is made to follow Penelope’s first.  That is Pe- followed by Di-.

The second hemistich is the same construction with *sequatur* ellipsed: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: the first syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus.  That is Ca- followed by Re-.

In the linear order required by the two *sequatur*’s we get therefore

Penelope’s first → Dido’s first → Cadmus’ first → Remus’ first syllable

Pe- Di- Ca- Re- = *pedic-are*.

*quodque fit ex illis* is the verb that is made out of those four beginnings, *pedicare*, *pedica-re* from *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, the stocks, the manacle for the feet’.  *pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the *pedica*, to fetter / shackle the feet, to put in the stocks.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the threat of the riddle: you who are *deprensus in horto*, thief caught in the garden, will give me/undergo what is made out of them, and with this *poena* your *culpa* is to be *luenda*.  The poena threatened to the *fur deprensus in horto* is the *pedicatio*: to be fettered, put in the stocks, to pay with the feet.  That is the classical gloss of the school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*; in the later vulgar transmission the same form is the familiar obscene reading of the garden-thief joke.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The grammatical core I am carrying forward is the nominative-accusative syntax of *sequatur*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nominative subject *Didonis prima*, accusative object *Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. By ellipsis the second hemistich is parallel: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nominative *syllaba prima Remi*, accusative *primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The verb therefore fixes a follow-order, not a simple left-to-right concatenation.

The dispute in round 2 is the meaning of *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima* and what the follow-order yields.

Pedicare camp – Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 – reads *primam/prima* as ‘first syllable’ throughout and keeps the verb as the ordering device but composes Pe- Di- Ca- Re- in the linear order Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus. That gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is then ‘you caught in the garden, thief, will give me/what is made out of them: with this penalty your guilt is to be atoned’. Classically the poena is being fettered/put in the stocks, in later vulgar transmission the familiar obscene *pedicatio* gloss of the garden-thief joke. Internal split in this camp between the literal *pedica* fetter/stocks reading and the vulgar sexual reading, and the Pen- vs Pe- problem: *Penelopes primam* as a first syllable would be *Pen-*, not *Pe-*.

Deprecare camp – Colleagues 1,12,13,14,5,7,9 – keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction and the subject-object order. *primam/prima* without *syllaba* is the first letter/element; only Remus is explicitly *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* gives P then D in the order the verb prescribes, and *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* gives C then Re, i.e. Re follows C. In the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses the four elements are D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. The pun *deprensus* : *deprecare* and the fact that *dare* fits *preces dare* is the aesthetic payoff. This reading respects the letter/syllable marking and avoids the Pen- / Pe- inconsistency; the cost is that it reverses the second block from the school tradition Ca-Re to Re-C and it requires *primam* = first letter.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether the author intended the strict syntactic/letter reading *deprecare* with supplication as the poena, or the conventional school charade *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pendicare* with fettering/stocks, and within the latter whether the classical *pedica* or the later vulgar *pedicatio* is the intended sense. My current working interpretation stays with the traditional syllabic charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, i.e. the thief is threatened with being fettered/put in the stocks, the form conventionally cited as the garden-thief’s *pedicatio*, while noting that the grammatical/lexical arguments for the *deprecare/deprecari* reading – subject-object order of *sequatur*, the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking, the Pen- vs Pe- problem, and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo – are strong and represent the strictly syntactic construal of the verse.

reflection_text.12:
The charade hinges on *sequatur* order and on *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima*.

Deprecare camp:
1,12,13,14,7,5,9 stress syntax. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: subject Didonis prima, object Penelopes primam → let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first → block D P. Second hemistich elided *sequatur*: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first → block Re C. With *primam* = first letter for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, and *syllaba prima* = syllable for Remus = Re-, the four elements in the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses are D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’. The pun *deprensus in horto* ~ *deprecare* and *dabis* ‘you will give’ fits *preces dare* better than ‘give a fetter’. The *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking is argued to be deliberate: poet only marks syllable for Remus; Penelope’s first syllable would be *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, so a consistent syllabic reading gives *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*, undermining Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Pedicare camp:
10,11,2,3,4,6,8 keep verse-order concatenation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *pedica* f. foot-fetter, stocks, *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/shackle feet, put in stocks. In later vulgar transmission the same form is glossed as the obscene *pedicatio*. They read *sequatur* as “let X follow Y in the order of mention” i.e. Penelope’s first then Dido’s first, Cadmus’ first then Remus’ first syllable → Pe-Di-Ca-Re. Some note the *deprensus:deprecare* echo is attractive but requires reversing the second block to Re-C and treating *primam* as first letter everywhere while keeping *syllaba prima* as syllable.

Internal tensions noted:
* Pe- vs Pen- inconsistency for Penelope: syllabic reading wants *Pen-*, which makes *pendicare* not *pedicare*.
* *primam* meaning: letter vs syllable. Deprecare camp says *primam* = first letter, *syllaba prima* marks the one true syllable. Pedicare camp says *primam* = first syllable, *syllaba prima* just confirms it for Remus.
* *dabis* semantics: *deprecare* can be given as *preces dare*; *pedica* is suffered, not given.
* Camp split on penalty meaning: literal *pedica* = stocks/fetter vs vulgar sexual *pedicatio*; deprecare camp unifies as supplication.

Current weight: syntactic/lexical argument for *deprecare/deprecari* — supplication, to beg pardon — is stronger on grammar and the deliberate *primam/syllaba prima* contrast and the *deprensus/deprecare* pun. The classical school gloss *pedicare* = fetter/stocks, with vulgar extension, remains the most frequent traditional citation and cannot be dismissed; it relies on verse-order concatenation and a looser reading of *sequatur*. Unresolved: whether the author intended consistent letter vs syllable marking, and whether *sequatur* should be read strictly as subject-object inversion or as poetic ordering in verse order.
reflection_text.3:
The riddle is a charade built from Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, Remus and sequatur governs the order.

Last round’s two camps remain.

Pedicare / pedica camp – Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8
* Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-.
* The two sequatur clauses are read as “let X follow Y” with the linear composition Pe then Di then Ca then Re.
* quodque fit ex illis = pedicare < pedica f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. 
* Poena = to be pedicated, fettered/shackled/put in stocks; in later vulgar transmission the familiar obscene pedicatio gloss. 
* Arguments: this is the familiar school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re; sequatur is consistently object then subject giving Pe then Di and Ca then Re; pedicare is a concrete penal action the fur can suffer.
* Internal tension noted: 11 glosses vulgar sodomy, 2,4,6,12 gloss classical fetter/stocks – not identical; also Pen- vs Pe- problem.

Deprecare / deprecari camp – Colleagues 1,12,13,14,5,7,9
* Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are marked primam/prima, only Remus is explicitly syllaba prima Remi = Re-.
* primam without syllaba = first letter/element, not first syllable. Penelopes primam is P not Pe-, and Penelope’s first syllable would be Pen-, not Pe-, hence Pe-Di-Ca-Re is unstable and slips to Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare.
* Syntax: Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam, subject Didonis prima, object Penelopes primam : let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. Same hyperbaton with sequatur elided in second hemistich: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi : let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.
* Order imposed by sequatur: first block D P, second block Re C. Together D P Re C = depreca-, deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’.
* Payoff: tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis quodque fit ex illis. The caught thief is condemned to give a deprecatio, to deprecari; deprensus : deprecare pun, and dare preces is something you can actually give, whereas dare a fetter is awkward. hac poena culpa luenda tua est fits supplication.
* Arguments for pedicare: sequatur consistently object then subject; the verse is the familiar school charade; deprecare needs primam = letter for three names and syllable for one and reverses second block to Re C.
* Arguments for deprecare: poet’s primam vs syllaba prima marking is deliberate; Pen- vs Pe- inconsistency; sequatur order kept intact; deprensus pun.

Unresolved: whether primam is uniformly first syllable/element or first letter with syllaba prima explicitly marked; whether second hemistich is Ca Re or Re C under sequatur; exact status of Penelope’s primam = Pe- vs Pen-; whether pedica = fetter/stocks vs vulgar pedicatio; whether the riddle intends physical pedica penalty or rhetorical penalty of deprecari.

My current synthesis: the primam/syllaba prima distinction and the subject-object order of sequatur are grammatically compelling for D-P-Re-C = deprecare with the deprensus pun, and the Pe- truncation / Pen- problem is a real weakness for the straight Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading. The pedicare reading remains the traditional school citation and the majority in round 0, but round 2 shows the grammatical/deprecare analysis is consistently reaffirmed by several colleagues on syntactic and marking grounds. Pending resolution of the primam meaning and the exact sequatur composition.
reflection_text.8:
The riddle is a charade controlled by *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* and the threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Two competing parses dominate the current discussion.

Reading A – verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare / pendicare.
* Penelopes primam = Pe-[Pen-], Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, taken in the order Pe-Di-Ca-Re.
* *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in the stocks.
* The penalty to the *fur deprensus in horto* is therefore to be pedicated/fettered. The camp splits on the nuance of *pedicare*: classical *pedica* stocks/fetter vs later vulgar *pedicatio* obscene sense, and on the first element Pen- vs Pe-, with Pen-Di-Ca-Re giving *pendicare*.
* Support cited is the usual scholastic gloss and the natural verse-order concatenation. Objections noted in round 2: it flattens *primam/prima* to first syllable everywhere, requires Pe- instead of Pen-, and must reverse the second hemistich order.

Reading B – strict syntax D P Re C = deprecare / deprecari.
* *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima* nom. sequitur *Penelopes primam* acc.: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first → D follows P.
* Second hemistich elided: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Remus’ first syllable follows Cadmus’ first → Re follows C.
* The poet marks *syllaba prima* only for Remus; *primam/prima* elsewhere is taken as first letter/element: P, D, C and explicit Re-. Order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses gives D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’.
* The pun *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare* and the verb *dabis* ‘you will give’ fits *preces dare* better than *dare* a fetter. *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is then atonement by supplication.
* Support cited: respects subject-object order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs, keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking, explains the *deprensus/deprecare* echo. Objections noted: it requires *primam* = first letter not first syllable, and moves away from the familiar school gloss Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Round 2 public positions keep the split. 1,12,13,7,9 argue for the strict *sequatur* + letter/syllable distinction yielding *deprecare* and the supplication penalty, pointing to Pe- vs Pen- inconsistency and the Re C order. 10,11,2,4,6,8 defend the traditional syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, with *pedica* fetter/stocks, acknowledging the *deprensus/deprecare* echo but treating it as rhetorical embellishment.

Unresolved: whether *primam/prima* means first letter or first syllable; whether Penelope’s first is Pe- or Pen-; whether *sequatur* is to be read as verse-order concatenation or as strict subject-object ordering giving D-P and Re-C; whether *dabis* is better satisfied by a physical penalty or by *preces dare*; whether the intended penalty is literal fettering/stocks, vulgar *pedicatio*, or supplication *deprecari*.

I retain both the traditional mass reading *pedicare* and the syntactically strict *deprecare* reading with its *deprensus* pun as live alternatives, with the tension being segmentation, order, and the *primam / syllaba prima* marking.
reflection_text.2:
The charade is built on Penelopes / Didonis / Cadmi / Remi and the dispute is primam/prima vs syllaba prima and how sequatur linearises.

Core pieces:
* Penelopes primam = Pe- / Pen- / P; Didonis prima = Di- / D; Cadmi primam = Ca- / C; Remi syllaba prima = Re- / R.
* Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp. Verse-order concatenation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare < pedica f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks’. Threat *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est* read as fettering/put in stocks; vulgar medieval gloss *pedicatio*. Support: straight verse order, canonical school tradition, concrete garden-thief penalty. Problems: primam would have to mean ‘first syllable’ everywhere but Penelope’s first syllable is Pen- not Pe- so the form is really Pendicare; primam vs syllaba prima distinction is ignored; order of second hemistich is treated as Ca-Re rather than Remus-follows-Cadmus.

* Deprecare/deprecari camp. Strict syntax: *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* = Dido’s first follows Penelope’s first; *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = Remus’ first syllable follows Cadmus’ first. With primam read as first letter and syllaba prima as explicit syllable we get P,D and Re,C in the order imposed by sequatur, i.e. D P Re C → depreca-/deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, beg pardon, give preces’. Support: primam vs syllaba prima distinction kept, deprensus/deprecare pun, dabis fits ‘give a prayer’ better than ‘give a fetter’. Problems: forces letter/syllable mix and reverses intuitive verse order; canonical gloss is pedicare.

Current state:
Round 0 majority pedicare, minority deprecare. Round 1 split persisted. Round 2 is ~7-7. Colleagues 12 and 5 switched from pedicare to deprecare on syntactic/primam vs syllaba grounds; colleagues 1,13,14,7,9 maintain/harden deprecare. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 maintain pedicare with verse-order sequatur reading Pe-Di then Ca-Re.

Unresolved cruxes remain: meaning of primam – first letter or first syllable – and Pen- vs Pe-; how sequatur is to be linearised – subject follows object gives object first then subject, which still yields Penelope→Dido, Cadmus→Remus, but deprecare camp reads concatenation as D P Re C to preserve subject-object order; whether dare a fetter vs dare preces is the intended fit, and the split within pedicare camp between classical pedica stocks/fetter and later vulgar pedicatio.

I continue to lean to the canonical majority pedicare/pedicatio as the intended school riddle, while recognising the strong syntactic case for deprecare/deprecari on sequatur ordering, the primam/syllaba prima marking, the deprensus echo, and the Pen- vs Pe- instability in the pedicare segmentation. The discussion is now essentially tied and the grammatical objection to verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re remains unresolved.
reflection_text.4:
The charade hinges on two interpretive choices: the syntactic force of *sequatur* and the meaning of *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima*.

Sequatur syntax:
* *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: subject *Didonis prima*, object *Penelopes primam*. Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.
* The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* ellipsed: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.

If the order imposed by the verb is kept, the blocks are D P for the first pair and Re C for the second pair, i.e. D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer *preces*’. That reading also preserves the author’s marking: *syllaba prima* is used only for Remus = Re-, while *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is the first letter P, D, C. The *deprensus in horto* / *deprecare* pun and the suitability of *dabis* for a prayer/supplication are the aesthetic payoff of this reading.

The traditional school reading keeps verse order Pe-Di-Ca-Re:
* *Penelopes primam* = Pe-, *Didonis prima* = Di-, *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- → Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.
* *pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis; *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/shackle, put in stocks. In later vulgar transmission the same form is glossed as the obscene *pedicatio*.

Instabilities in the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp:
* Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, so Pe-Di-Ca-Re forces *Pen-* → *Pendicare* in 5,7,13. The segmentation is stretched.
* The camp splits on meaning: classical *pedica* fetter/stocks 2,4,6,10,12 vs vulgar sodomy 11.
* To get Pe-Di-Ca-Re the second hemistich order must be reversed from the syntax Re C to Ca Re, and *primam* must be read as first syllable for Penelope/Dido/Cadmus while *syllaba prima* is kept for Remus.

Disagreements in round 2:
Colleagues 1,12,13,14,5,7,9 keep the subject-object order of *sequatur* and the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction and arrive at *deprecare*, with the penalty of being forced to give supplication/pardon-begging, the *deprensus*:*deprecare* echo.
Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 read *sequatur* in verse order Pe→Di and Ca→Re and arrive at *pedicare/pendicare*, penalty = fettering/stocks, traditionally cited as the garden-thief punishment, later vulgarised.

Unresolved: whether the riddle author intended strict Latin syntax and letter/syllable marking, giving *deprecare*, or the conventional school charade convention where *sequatur* is taken as linear concatenation and *primam* = first syllable, giving *pedicare/pendicare*. The grammatical argument for *deprecare* is strong; the manuscript/traditional citation weight is for *pedicare*.
reflection_text.11:
The riddle is a charade with two *sequatur* clauses and a final threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Deprecare camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,9,12,13,14 – keeps the Latin syntax and the author’s marking. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: subject Dido’s first, object Penelope’s first, ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* ellipsed: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. The poet marks *syllaba prima* only for Remus; *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is read as first letter, not first syllable. That avoids the Pen- vs Pe- problem: Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not *Pe-*; forcing a syllable reading everywhere gives *Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare*.

With *primam* = first letter P,D,C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, and the follow-order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses, the blocks are D P and Re C, i.e. D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’. The pun *deprensus in horto* ~ *deprecare* and the verb *dabis* ‘you will give’ fits *preces dare* much better than giving a fetter. The penalty is supplication / begging pardon.

Pedicare camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,10,11 – reads *primam* systematically as first syllable, with *syllaba prima* simply confirming the syllable status for Remus. In the verse order they take

*Penelopes primam = Pe-*, *Didonis prima = Di-*, *primam Cadmi = Ca-*, *syllaba prima Remi = Re-*

and with *sequatur* taken as “let X follow Y” in linear composition order they get Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis; *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in the stocks. The threat is the garden thief will be *pedicatus*, fettered/put in stocks. The camp is internally split: 11,12,14, etc. gloss the form with the later vulgar *pedicatio* / sodomy sense, while 2,4,6,12 gloss it classically as fetters/stocks.

The split persists:

* primam vs *syllaba prima*: does the author signal first letter vs first syllable? Deprecare camp says yes, pedicare camp says *primam* = first syllable throughout and *syllaba prima* is explicit confirmation.
* Sequatur ordering: deprecare camp insists subject follows object, giving D after P and Re after C, i.e. D P Re C. Pedicare camp reads the clauses as composition order Pe then Di and Ca then Re, i.e. Pe Di Ca Re, and claims the syntax can be accommodated.
* Pen- vs Pe-: syllable reading of Penelope gives *Pen-*, forcing *pendicare*; pedicare camp truncates to *Pe-*.
* Semantics of *dabis* and *hac poena*: deprecare camp stresses *dare preces* is gift-like and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo is the riddle’s payoff; pedicare camp stresses traditional school gloss *pedicare* as the garden-theft joke, with literal fetter vs vulgar sexual divergence unresolved.

Round 2 shows no convergence. Colleague 10,11 now explicitly reconcile *sequatur* with the Pe-Di-Ca-Re order, while Colleague 12,13,14,7,9,5,1 reaffirm the grammatical *primam/syllaba prima* distinction and the D P Re C order. The core unresolved question remains whether the verse intends the strict grammatical charade *deprecare/deprecari* with supplication as the poena, or the traditional school charade *pedicare/pendicare* with fettering/stocks – and in the latter case whether it is the literal *pedica* or the vulgar *pedicatio*.
reflection_text.6:
The syntactic frame is now stable: *sequatur* is 3sg subjunctive with nominative subject following accusative object.

First hemistich: *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* = ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. Object first in wording, subject second in execution → Penelope first, Dido second in the final string. Second hemistich with *sequatur* elided: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. → Cadmus first, Remus second. Nominal order of composition is therefore Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus, i.e. P D C Re.

The fork is segmentation + marking.

Pedicare camp, 10,11,2,4,6,8,3: *primam/prima* = first syllable for all four names, *syllaba prima* is explicit emphasis for Remus only. With P D C Re that gives Pe- Di- Ca- Re- = *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *quodque fit ex illis* is the verb *pedicare*, ‘to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle’. The threatened *poena* is fettering/putting in stocks; later vulgar transmission glosses it with the obscene *pedicatio* sense. Camp notes the traditional school citation and that *dabis* can be read as undergo the penalty. Internal tension: Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, so *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* requires truncation; several colleagues slide to *Pendicare* = *Pen-Di-Ca-Re*.

Deprecare camp, 1,12,13,14,5,7,9: *primam/prima* is first letter/element, *syllaba prima* is the only true syllable marker. Hence Penelope = P, Dido = D, Cadmus = C, Remus = Re-. Keeping the *sequatur* order strictly, subject follows object, gives first block P then D and second block C then Re in the lineal string, but read in the natural subject-object direction the charade is assembled as D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, give *preces*’. This respects the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* asymmetry and yields the neat *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare* echo, and *dare preces* is something you can materially *dare*. They argue *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* needs two incompatible fixes: read *primam* as syllable for Penelope/Dido but as letter for Cadmus, and reverse the second hemistich from Re C to Ca Re, plus force *Pe-* from *Pen-*.

Current state after round 2: syntactic order is accepted by both sides, disagreement is whether *primam* means first letter or first syllable. The *primam / syllaba prima* marking is now the central crux, with 1,12,13,14 arguing it decides for deprecare, and 10,11,2,4,6 arguing for traditional syllabic pedicare/pendicare. The pedicare camp is internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks and vulgar obscene gloss. Unresolved is whether the riddle intends the literal legal punishment of fettering or the supplication punishment, and whether the *deprensus/deprecare* pun is authorial or a later rhetorical embellishment.

reflection_text.10:
The grammatical core I am carrying forward is the nominative-accusative syntax of *sequatur*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nominative subject *Didonis prima*, accusative object *Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. By ellipsis the second hemistich is parallel: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nominative *syllaba prima Remi*, accusative *primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The verb therefore fixes a follow-order, not a simple left-to-right concatenation.

The dispute in round 2 is the meaning of *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima* and what the follow-order yields.

Pedicare camp – Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8 – reads *primam/prima* as ‘first syllable’ throughout and keeps the verb as the ordering device but composes Pe- Di- Ca- Re- in the linear order Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus. That gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is then ‘you caught in the garden, thief, will give me/what is made out of them: with this penalty your guilt is to be atoned’. Classically the poena is being fettered/put in the stocks, in later vulgar transmission the familiar obscene *pedicatio* gloss of the garden-thief joke. Internal split in this camp between the literal *pedica* fetter/stocks reading and the vulgar sexual reading, and the Pen- vs Pe- problem: *Penelopes primam* as a first syllable would be *Pen-*, not *Pe-*.

Deprecare camp – Colleagues 1,12,13,14,5,7,9 – keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction and the subject-object order. *primam/prima* without *syllaba* is the first letter/element; only Remus is explicitly *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* gives P then D in the order the verb prescribes, and *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* gives C then Re, i.e. Re follows C. In the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses the four elements are D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. The pun *deprensus* : *deprecare* and the fact that *dare* fits *preces dare* is the aesthetic payoff. This reading respects the letter/syllable marking and avoids the Pen- / Pe- inconsistency; the cost is that it reverses the second block from the school tradition Ca-Re to Re-C and it requires *primam* = first letter.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether the author intended the strict syntactic/letter reading *deprecare* with supplication as the poena, or the conventional school charade *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pendicare* with fettering/stocks, and within the latter whether the classical *pedica* or the later vulgar *pedicatio* is the intended sense. My current working interpretation stays with the traditional syllabic charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, i.e. the thief is threatened with being fettered/put in the stocks, the form conventionally cited as the garden-thief’s *pedicatio*, while noting that the grammatical/lexical arguments for the *deprecare/deprecari* reading – subject-object order of *sequatur*, the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking, the Pen- vs Pe- problem, and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo – are strong and represent the strictly syntactic construal of the verse.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The marking the poet gives us is doing grammatical work and it is hard to set aside.

*Penelopes primam*, *Didonis prima*, *primam Cadmi* are all given with *primam/prima* alone. Only Remus is explicitly *syllaba prima Remi*. That is the normal Latin way to signal first letter/element with *primam/prima* and first syllable with *syllaba prima*. If *primam* were meant as ‘first syllable’ everywhere we would have *Pen-* from Penelope, not *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain would already collapse into Pen-Di-Ca-Re. The text avoids that by reserving *syllaba prima* for the one case where a syllable is actually required, Re-.

The verb then fixes the order in both hemistichs. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: the subject is *Didonis prima*, the object *Penelopes primam*, ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. The block prescribed by the verb is D followed by P, not the linear verse order P then D.

The second hemistich is the exact parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*, ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. That is Re followed by C.

In the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe we therefore have D P Re C, *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’. It is the only reading that keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction intact and respects the follow-order in both hemistichs.

It also gives the riddle its aesthetic payoff. *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief is *deprensus* and is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces. *Preces dare* is something you can give, and the verse says with this *poena* your *culpa* is to be *luenda*. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is exactly the kind of internal pun the charade is built on.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp needs two incompatible adjustments at once: it has to read *primam* as syllable for Penelope and Dido but as letter for Cadmus, it has to reverse the second hemistich from Re C to Ca Re, and it is internally split. 11 glosses the same form with the later vulgar sexual sense *pedicatio*, while 2,4,6,10 gloss it with the classical *pedica* fetter/stocks. Those are not the same penalty, and the Pe- vs Pen- instability shows the segmentation is being stretched to a familiar word.

10 and 3 themselves note that the strict grammatical reading of the two *sequatur* clauses yields D P Re C, and then retreat to “ordinary tradition” for *pedicare*. Once the author’s own *primam / syllaba prima* marking and the subject-object order of *sequatur* are kept consistently, the charade is *deprecare* and the poena the fur must give is the supplication, the *deprecatio* that echoes *deprensus*.
