3.text:
The order is set by *sequatur* and by the way the verse marks letter against syllable.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*. Nom. *Didonis prima* is the subject, acc. *Penelopes primam* the object: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. The first block is therefore P then D in the order of composition, D P when the verb is read in its natural subject-object direction.

The second hemistich is the exact parallel with *sequatur* understood:

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*.

Nom. *syllaba prima Remi* is the subject, acc. *primam Cadmi* the object: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. The second block is therefore C then Re in the order of composition, Re C when the verb is read in its natural direction.

The poet marks the distinction deliberately. He says *syllaba prima* once, with Remus, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. *primam / prima / primam* for Penelope, Dido and Cadmus is left unmarked by *syllaba*. That is the normal Latin signal for first letter/ first element, not first syllable. If *primam* were meant as first syllable everywhere we would have *Pen-* from Penelope, not *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re segmentation would already be *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*.

Keeping the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking and the subject-object order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses we have

*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* : D P
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* : Re C

D P Re C = *depreca-*.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’. The verse then gives the pun on which the riddle is built:

*mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis… hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

The *fur* who is *deprensus in horto* is condemned to *dare* what is made out of the pieces, and what can be *datum* is a *deprecatio*. *Deprensus : deprecare* is the internal echo of the riddle and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is exactly the poetic way of saying the guilt is atoned by supplication.

That is the reading that respects both the *primam / syllaba prima* distinction and the follow-order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs. On the familiar scholastic syllabic verse-order reading *primam / prima* is taken as ‘first syllable’ throughout and the order of the second hemistich is reversed to Ca Re, giving Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, *manica pedis*’, i.e. classically ‘to be pedicated, fettered/put in the stocks’, the form which in later vulgar transmission is the familiar obscene gloss of the garden-thief joke.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ve been re-reading the two sequatur clauses carefully and I think the *primam / syllaba prima* marking is doing real syntactic work, not just decorative.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is nominative + accusative: *Didonis prima* is the subject that is made to follow *Penelopes primam*. The verb tells us the order in the composition is Penelope’s first followed by Dido’s first, so the first block the verse commands is P then D. The same ellipse is at work in the second hemistich: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. The subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, the object is *primam Cadmi*: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. That is Re followed by C in the order the verb prescribes.

The poet is explicit about what is a syllable and what is not. He says *syllaba prima* once, and only for Remus. Penelope, Dido and Cadmus are all given plain *primam / prima*. In the normal Latin charade use *prima* without *syllaba* signals the first element, the first letter, while *syllaba prima* signals an actual syllable. Keeping the marking consistent we get P, D from the first clause and Re, C from the second clause in the order imposed by the two *sequatur*s: D follows P and Re follows C, i.e. D P Re C in the natural subject-object reading of the verb. That is *depreca-*.

That also gives the riddle its internal echo. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief is *deprensus* and he is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces. *Dare* preces is a normal collocation, *deprecare / deprecari* is ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is exactly the poetic way of saying the guilt is atoned by supplication. A fetter is something you suffer, not something you *dabis* in that sense, and the *deprensus : deprecare* pun is the aesthetic payoff the verse is built around.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* reading has to flatten the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction, reverse the second *sequatur* from Re C to Ca Re, and force *Penelopes primam* to be *Pe-* instead of the expected *Pen-*. The *sequatur* clauses are the ordering machine and the two hemistichs are parallel.

primam Cadmi = Ca-
syllaba prima Remi = Re-

Ca- + Re- = Ca-Re-.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The ordering really is set by the two *sequatur* clauses and the way the poet marks what he wants.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is the regular acc. + nom. + subj. construction: *Didonis prima* is nominative subject, *Penelopes primam* accusative object. ‘Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.’ The first piece to be placed in the charade is the one that is followed, Penelope’s, and the piece that follows it is Dido’s. The same ellipse is at work in the second hemistich. *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.’ So Cadmus’ first is the one that is followed and Remus’ first syllable is the follower.

That gives us two blocks in the order the verbs prescribe: P followed by D, and C followed by Re. In the linear order of the *sequatur* the pieces come out D P Re C.

The marking confirms it. The poet says *syllaba prima* once, and only for Remus. *Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are all left without *syllaba*. In Latin charade usage *prima/primam* without *syllaba* is the signal for the first letter / first element, not the first syllable. If he wanted a syllable for Penelope he would have written *syllaba prima Penelopes* just as he does for Remus. *Penelopes primam* is therefore P, not *Pen-* and certainly not the truncated *Pe-* that the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation needs. The same goes for Dido and Cadmus: D and C, not *Di-* and *Ca-* as syllables. The only syllable we are licensed to take is Re- from *syllaba prima Remi*.

With primam = first letter and the *sequatur* order respected we get D P + Re C = *depreca-*. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’.

That is the reading the verse rewards internally. *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief who is *deprensus* is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces, and *hac poena* his guilt is to be *luenda*. You *dare preces*; you *deprecare*. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is exactly the kind of pun a school charade sets up, and it makes *dabis* natural: you give supplication, you are condemned to entreaty. It also removes the *Pen-* vs *Pe-* strain that forces the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp into a mixed letter/syllable reading and into the Re-C → Ca-Re reversal in the second hemistich.

Once *primam* is kept as first letter and *sequatur* is kept parallel in both hemistichs, the charade is cleanly *depreca-*, and the penalty named for the *fur deprensus in horto* is the obligation to *deprecare*, to make supplication for pardon.

*pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the *pedica*, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in the stocks. 

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is therefore the threat of the riddle: you who are *deprensus in horto*, thief caught in the garden, will give/undergo what is made out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re, and with this *poena* your *culpa* is to be *luenda*.

Classically the *poena* named is the *pedica*: the *fur deprensus in horto* is threatened with being *pedicatus*, with being fettered/put in the stocks, i.e. to pay with the feet. That is the *Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare* school charade on which the familiar vulgar transmission of the hortus joke is built.

In Latin charade usage that is the signal for first element/letter, not first syllable. Unresolved: authorial intent for strict Latin syntax and letter/syllable marking giving *deprecare* vs conventional school charade convention where *sequatur* is taken as linear concatenation and *primam* = first syllable, giving the manuscript/traditional *pedicare*. The camp notes that the *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* reading requires flattening *primam* vs *syllaba prima*, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and smoothing *Pen-* to *Pe-*.

*Pedicare* camp, 11,2,6,8 and partly 10: *primam/prima* is read as first syllable throughout, *syllaba prima* is emphatic for Remus only. Classical gloss is fettering/putting in stocks, later vulgar tradition glosses with obscene *pedicatio*. The camp argues the school tradition is the citation, *sequatur* is read left-to-right in verse order, and the *Pen-* vs *Pe-* objection is dismissed by taking *Pe-* as conventional truncation.

Current state after round 3: syntactic order is accepted by both sides; disagreement remains primam = first letter vs first syllable and whether the author’s *primam / syllaba prima* contrast and the *sequatur* subject-object order are to be kept consistently. The *deprecare* reading is now heavily reinforced for grammatical consistency and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo and *dare preces* plausibility. The *pedicare* reading retains the weight of traditional school citation and the Pe-Di-Ca-Re form, but is internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks and vulgar obscene gloss, and requires inconsistent handling of *primam* and reversal of the second *sequatur* block.

Unresolved: whether the riddle intends the literal legal punishment of fettering or supplication, and whether the *deprensus/deprecare* pun is authorial or rhetorical embellishment of the traditional charade. The *primam / syllaba prima* marking remains the central crux.

Reading A – verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare / pendicare*.

Reading B – strict syntax D P Re C = *deprecare / deprecari*.

Round 3 public positions:
1 now argues strictly for *deprecare* on *primam / syllaba prima* marking and *sequatur* order, noting Pe-Di-Ca-Re needs incompatible adjustments.
10,12,13,14,7,5,9 maintain the strict grammatical reading D P Re C = *deprecare*, while acknowledging the traditional school gloss *pedicare* as the verse-order concatenation that flattens the marking.
11,2,6,8 defend the traditional syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, with *pedica* fetter/stocks classically and *pedicatio* vulgarly; 2,3,4 also note the syntactic elegance of the *deprecare* reading but keep the traditional citation.

Unresolved: whether *primam/prima* means first letter or first syllable; whether Penelope’s first is Pe- or Pen-; whether *sequatur* is to be read as verse-order concatenation or as strict subject-object ordering giving D-P and Re-C; whether *dabis* is better satisfied by a physical penalty or by *preces dare*; whether intended penalty is literal fettering/stocks, vulgar *pedicatio*, or supplication *deprecari*.

My current weighting is shifting toward the syntactically strict *deprecare* reading because of the poet’s explicit *syllaba prima* marking only for Remus and the parallel *sequatur* construction, and the internal *deprensus/deprecare* pun, while retaining the traditional *pedicare* = *pedica* fetter/stocks gloss and its later vulgar development as the historically cited school answer.

reflection_text.4:
The riddle is a charade controlled by *sequatur* and by the poet’s marking of *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima*.

Strict syntactic reading:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. subject *Didonis prima* follows acc. object *Penelopes primam*. Block 1 order prescribed by the verb is P → D.
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi*. Block 2 order is C → Re.
Marking: *syllaba prima* is said once and only for Remus = Re-; *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is unmarked by *syllaba*. In Latin charade usage that is the signal for first element/letter, not first syllable. If *primam* were first syllable everywhere Penelope would give *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, so the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re would collapse to *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*.
With primam = first letter P D C and syllaba prima = Re-, the verb order gives D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’. The closure *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is then the *deprensus : deprecare* pun; *dare preces* is apt and *hac poena culpa luenda* fits atonement by supplication. This is the reading defended by colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,7,9,5.

Traditional school reading:
Verse-order concatenation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *Primam/prima* read as first syllable for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, with *syllaba prima* explicit for Remus to secure Re-. *sequatur* taken as linear list, not as subject-object order, and the second hemistich reversed to Ca-Re to get verse order. *pedica* f. = foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis; *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/put in stocks. Classical gloss = being fettered/put in stocks for the garden thief; later vulgar transmission glosses the same form as *pedicatio*.
This is defended by colleagues 11,2,4,6,8,12 with the split in meaning: classical fetter/stocks 2,4,6,10,12 vs vulgar sodomy 11.

Instabilities in the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp:
Pen- vs Pe- strain; need to flatten *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction; need to reverse Re C to Ca Re; internal split on meaning of *pedicare*.
Disagreement in round 3: 10,1,12,13,14,7,9 maintain the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction and subject-object *sequatur* → *deprecare*; 11,2,4,6,8 maintain the traditional verse-order syllabic charade → *pedicare*, with 2,3,4,8 explicitly noting the strict syntactic parsing gives *deprecare* but reverting to tradition as the cited gloss.

Unresolved: authorial intent for strict Latin syntax and letter/syllable marking giving *deprecare* vs conventional school charade convention where *sequatur* is taken as linear concatenation and *primam* = first syllable, giving the manuscript/traditional *pedicare*. The grammatical argument for *deprecare* is strong; the weight of citation is for *pedicare*.
reflection_text.6:
The syntactic frame is settled across both camps: *sequatur* is 3sg subjunctive with nominative subject following accusative object. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. Second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. Order prescribed by the verbs is therefore first block P then D, second block C then Re; in subject-object direction D P Re C.

The remaining fork is segmentation + marking.

*Deprecare* camp, 1,10,12,13,14,3,4,5,7,9: *primam/prima* without *syllaba* is the normal charade signal for first letter/element, *syllaba prima* is the explicit syllable marker used once for Remus. Hence Penelope = P, Dido = D, Cadmus = C, Remus = Re-. *Penelopes primam* would be *Pen-* if *primam* were first syllable, not *Pe-*, so Pe-Di-Ca-Re needs truncation/unstable *Pen-* vs *Pe-*. Keeping the marking intact and the subject-object order of both *sequatur* clauses gives D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer *preces*’. This yields the internal pun *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare*, and *dare preces* is a natural *dabis*; *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is atonement by supplication. The camp notes that the *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* reading requires flattening *primam* vs *syllaba prima*, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and smoothing *Pen-* to *Pe-*.

*Pedicare* camp, 11,2,6,8 and partly 10: *primam/prima* is read as first syllable throughout, *syllaba prima* is emphatic for Remus only. Verse-order concatenation gives Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re- → Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare* ‘to put in the pedica, to fetter/shackle’. Classical gloss is fettering/putting in stocks, later vulgar tradition glosses with obscene *pedicatio*. The camp argues the school tradition is the citation, *sequatur* is read left-to-right in verse order, and the *Pen-* vs *Pe-* objection is dismissed by taking *Pe-* as conventional truncation.

Current state after round 3: syntactic order is accepted by both sides; disagreement remains primam = first letter vs first syllable and whether the author’s *primam / syllaba prima* contrast and the *sequatur* subject-object order are to be kept consistently. The *deprecare* reading is now heavily reinforced for grammatical consistency and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo and *dare preces* plausibility. The *pedicare* reading retains the weight of traditional school citation and the Pe-Di-Ca-Re form, but is internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks and vulgar obscene gloss, and requires inconsistent handling of *primam* and reversal of the second *sequatur* block.

Unresolved: whether the riddle intends the literal legal punishment of fettering or supplication, and whether the *deprensus/deprecare* pun is authorial or rhetorical embellishment of the traditional charade. The *primam / syllaba prima* marking remains the central crux.
reflection_text.12:
The charade is still contested between a strict syntactic/letter-marking reading and the traditional verse-order syllabic reading.

Deprecare camp, colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,7,5,3,4,9:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. subject *Didonis prima* follows acc. object *Penelopes primam*. Second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi*.
The poet marks material: *syllaba prima* is said once, only for Remus = Re-. *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is taken as first element/letter, P, D, C. If *primam* were first syllable throughout Penelope would give *Pen-* not *Pe-*, collapsing Pe-Di-Ca-Re into *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*.
In the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses: D follows P, Re follows C → D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer *preces*’. This gives the internal pun *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare* and makes *dabis* natural as *preces dare*. *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* = atonement by supplication.

Pedicare camp, colleagues 2,6,8,11:
Verse-order concatenation Pe- Di- Ca- Re = *pedicare*. *primam/prima* read as first syllable throughout; *syllaba prima* just confirms Remus. *sequatur* read as “let X follow Y in order of mention” giving Pe then Di, Ca then Re. *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’, *pedicae dare* to fetter/shackle. Classical gloss = being put in stocks/fettered. Colleague 11 pushes later vulgar transmission *pedicatio*/*pedicari*. Colleagues 2,6,8 acknowledge the *deprensus:deprecare* echo is attractive but hold tradition.

Internal tensions retained:
* Pe- vs Pen- inconsistency for Penelope if syllabic.
* *primam* meaning letter vs syllable; deliberate contrast *primam* vs *syllaba prima*.
* *dabis* semantics: *deprecare* can be given as *preces dare*; *pedica* is suffered.
* Camp split on penalty meaning: literal fetter/stocks vs vulgar sexual sense vs supplication.

Current weight remains with the grammatically coherent deprecare reading because it respects the *primam* / *syllaba prima* distinction, the subject-object order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs, and the *deprensus:deprecare* pun. The traditional Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* citation persists and cannot be dismissed; it relies on flattening the marking distinction, reversing the second block Re C → Ca Re, and a verse-order concatenation. Unresolved is whether the author intended the strict letter/syllable marking or a loose school syllabic charade, and whether *sequatur* is to be taken strictly syntactically or poetically.
reflection_text.8:
The riddle is *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Two readings stay live, now more sharply articulated around *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima* and the subject-object order of *sequatur*.

Reading A – verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare / pendicare*.
* Penelopes primam = Pe-/Pen-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, taken in linear verse order.
* *quodque fit ex illis* → *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’; classically *pedicae dare* = to fetter / put in stocks. Later vulgar transmission is read as the obscene *pedicatio*.
* Support: familiar school charade, *syllaba prima* used to secure Re-, *primam/prima* used syllabically for the other three names.
* Objections raised repeatedly in round 3: Pe- vs Pen- instability; *primam* would then need to be first syllable for Penelope/Dido but first letter for Cadmus; second hemistich must be reversed from Re C to Ca Re to get Ca-Re; the camp is internally split between classical *pedica* stocks/fetter 2,4,6,8,12 and vulgar *pedicatio* 11; *dabis* is less natural for a fetter than for *preces dare*.

Reading B – strict syntax D P Re C = *deprecare / deprecari*.
* *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. *Didonis prima* follows acc. *Penelopes primam* → D follows P.
* Second hemistich elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi* → Re follows C.
* The poet marks material: *syllaba prima* is said once and only for Remus → Re-; *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is the normal charade signal for first element/letter → P, D, C.
* Order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses gives D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer *preces*’.
* The pun *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare* and *dabis* = *preces dare* fits well; *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* = atonement by supplication.
* Support cited in round 3 by 1,10,12,13,14,5,7,9: keeps *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction intact, respects parallel *sequatur* construction, avoids Pen- vs Pe- strain, explains *deprensus/deprecare* echo.
* Objections noted: requires *primam* = first letter not first syllable; moves away from familiar school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Round 3 public positions:
1 now argues strictly for *deprecare* on *primam / syllaba prima* marking and *sequatur* order, noting Pe-Di-Ca-Re needs incompatible adjustments.
10,12,13,14,7,5,9 maintain the strict grammatical reading D P Re C = *deprecare*, while acknowledging the traditional school gloss *pedicare* as the verse-order concatenation that flattens the marking.
11,2,6,8 defend the traditional syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, with *pedica* fetter/stocks classically and *pedicatio* vulgarly; 2,3,4 also note the syntactic elegance of the *deprecare* reading but keep the traditional citation.
3,4,8 note that the *deprensus : deprecare* echo is attractive rhetorical reinforcement even while citing the traditional gloss.

Unresolved: whether *primam/prima* means first letter or first syllable; whether Penelope’s first is Pe- or Pen-; whether *sequatur* is to be read as verse-order concatenation or as strict subject-object ordering giving D-P and Re-C; whether *dabis* is better satisfied by a physical penalty or by *preces dare*; whether intended penalty is literal fettering/stocks, vulgar *pedicatio*, or supplication *deprecari*.

My current weighting is shifting toward the syntactically strict *deprecare* reading because of the poet’s explicit *syllaba prima* marking only for Remus and the parallel *sequatur* construction, and the internal *deprensus/deprecare* pun, while retaining the traditional *pedicare* = *pedica* fetter/stocks gloss and its later vulgar development as the historically cited school answer.
reflection_text.3:
The riddle is a charade whose interpretation hinges on primam/prima vs syllaba prima and on the subject-object order of sequatur.

Primam / syllaba prima marking
* The poet marks Remus explicitly syllaba prima Remi = Re-. Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are all given without syllaba. Colleagues 1,10,12,13,14,5,7,9 argue this is the normal Latin charade signal: primam/prima = first element / first letter, syllaba prima = first syllable. If primam were uniformly ‘first syllable’ Penelopes primam would be Pen-, not Pe-, and Pe-Di-Ca-Re collapses to Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. That Pen- vs Pe- strain is repeatedly noted as a weakness for the syllabic reading.
* The Pedicare camp 11,2,6,8 keeps primam = first syllable for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus and takes syllaba prima for Remus as the same syllabic instruction. 2 and 6 claim Penelopes primam = Pe-, not Pen-, so the objection does not arise.

Sequatur order
* Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam. Nom. Didonis prima subject, acc. Penelopes primam object: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first. Second hemistich is parallel with sequatur elided: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi: nom. syllaba prima Remi subject, acc. primam Cadmi object: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.
* On a strict grammatical reading the order prescribed by the verbs is P→D and C→Re. In the natural subject-object direction the composition is D P Re C = depreca-, deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’. This reading is argued by 1,10,12,13,14,5,7,3,4,9 and gives the internal pun deprensus : deprecare and makes dabis natural: dare preces.
* The linear verse-order reading taken by the Pedicare camp keeps the pieces in the order they are named: Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus, Pe- Di- Ca- Re- = pedicare < pedica f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. 11,2,6,8 maintain that is the scholastic syllabic charade and the tradition under which the riddle is cited. They read sequatur as simply indicating succession in the verse, not reversing subject-object.

Punishment content
* Deprecare camp: poena is supplication, the obligation to deprecari, to give a deprecatio and beg pardon. hac poena culpa luenda tua est fits atonement by prayer, and deprensus/deprecare is the aesthetic payoff.
* Pedicare camp: quodque fit ex illis is pedicare. Classically pedicae dare, to be fettered/put in stocks, the garden thief’s penal action. Camp is internally split: 11 glosses later vulgar pedicatio / sodomy, 2,4,6,12 gloss classical pedica fetter/stocks. Both are developments of Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Current status
* Syntactic and marking evidence for D P Re C = deprecare is consistently reaffirmed in round 3 by 1,10,12,13,14,5,7,9 and acknowledged even by 3 and 4 as the grammatically coherent reading, with 10,3,4 noting the traditional pedicare gloss as a verse-order flattening.
* The traditional school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare remains the majority round 0 position and is defended in round 3 by 11,2,6,8. Their defense requires flattening primam vs syllaba prima, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and accepting Pe- for Penelope.
* Unresolved: whether the poet intended the strict subject-object sequatur with primam = first letter, or the familiar school syllable chain; exact semantic scope of pedicare = classical fetter/stocks vs vulgar transmission; whether deprensus pun is decisive or decorative.

My synthesis has moved toward the deprecare reading as the grammatically faithful construal that respects the poet’s own primam / syllaba prima contrast and the parallel sequatur clauses, while retaining pedicare < pedica as the traditional verse-order gloss that dominates the citation tradition.
reflection_text.11:
The riddle is a charade with *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Deprecare camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,9,10,12,13,14 and now 3,4 with qualification – keeps the poet’s own marking: *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus and *syllaba prima* only for Remus. *Primam* without *syllaba* is the normal Latin charade signal for first element/letter, P D C, while *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-. If *primam* were uniformly ‘first syllable’ Penelope would give *Pen-* not *Pe-*, so Pe-Di-Ca-Re collapses to Pen-Di-Ca-Re = *pendicare*, the Pen-/Pe- strain.

Sequatur is parallel in both hemistichs. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. subject *Didonis prima* follows acc. object *Penelopes primam*: P → D. Second hemistich ellipsed: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi*: C → Re. In subject-object direction the composition is D P Re C = *de-pre-ca-*.

*deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’. The payoff is the *deprensus : deprecare* echo and *dabis* = *preces dare*. *Hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is atonement by supplication. That reading keeps *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinct and the subject-object order of both *sequatur* clauses.

Pedicare camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,10,11,12 – reads *primam* systematically as first syllable, *syllaba prima* as explicit confirmation for Remus. Verse-order concatenation is Pe- Di- Ca- Re- = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in stocks. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore the *pedica* the *fur deprensus in horto* is told he will give/undergo. Camp is internally split: 2,4,6,8,10,12 give classical *pedica*/stocks; 11 gives vulgar *pedicatio* / sodomy as garden-thief joke.

Core disagreements persisting from earlier rounds:
* primam vs syllaba prima distinction: deprecare camp says it signals letter vs syllable; pedicare camp says primam = syllable throughout and *syllaba prima* is mere confirmation.
* sequatur ordering: deprecare camp insists subject follows object giving D P and Re C; pedicare camp reads linear verse order Pe-Di and Ca-Re.
* Pen- vs Pe-: syllable reading of Penelope gives *Pen-*, forcing *pendicare*; pedicare camp truncates to *Pe-*.
* Semantics of *dabis* and *hac poena*: deprecare camp stresses *dare preces* is give-able and the deprensus/deprecare pun; pedicare camp stresses traditional school gloss.

Round 3 shows no convergence. Colleagues 10,12,13,14,1,5,7,9,3,4 now explicitly argue the strict grammatical reading yields D P Re C = *deprecare* and note the traditional Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* is the verse-order flattening that reverses Re C to Ca Re. Colleagues 2,6,8,11 continue to defend Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* as the citation, with 2 and 3 acknowledging the grammatical elegance of *deprecare*.

Unresolved question remains whether the author intended the strict syntactic charade *deprecare* with punishment = supplication/beg pardon/give preces, or the traditional school charade *pedicare/pendicare* with punishment = fettering/stocks, and in the latter case literal *pedica* or vulgar *pedicatio*. The marking and parallelism favours the deprecare reading, but the traditional citation is pedicare.
reflection_text.10:
The grammatical core I am carrying forward is the nominative-accusative syntax of *sequatur* and the poet’s own marking of material.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nominative subject *Didonis prima*, accusative object *Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. By ellipsis the second hemistich is parallel: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nominative *syllaba prima Remi*, accusative *primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The verb therefore fixes a follow-order, not simple left-to-right concatenation.

The *primam / prima* vs *syllaba prima* distinction is now the decisive evidence. *Syllaba prima* is said once, only for Remus = Re-. *Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are left without *syllaba*. In Latin charade use *prima/primam* without *syllaba* signals first element / first letter, *syllaba prima* signals an explicit syllable. If *primam* were first syllable throughout Penelope would give *Pen-*, not *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain collapses to *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is repeatedly flagged by 1,5,7,13,14.

In the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses the four elements are:
*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → D follows P
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re follows C

With *primam* = first letter P, D, C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- this is D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’. The internal pun is *deprensus* : *deprecare* and *dare preces* = *dabis* in *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. Supplication fits *dare* and *culpa luenda* by prayer.

Pedica camp – 11,8,6,2 – reads *primam/prima* as ‘first syllable’ throughout and keeps the verb as ordering device but composes in linear verse order Penelope → Dido → Cadmus → Remus = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. *quodque fit ex illis* is then the fetter to be given/undergone. Classically this is being fettered/put in the stocks; in later vulgar transmission the familiar obscene *pedicatio* gloss of the garden-thief joke. This reading requires flattening the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* contrast, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and accepting the Pen- → Pe- truncation. The camp is internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks 2,4,6,10,12 and vulgar *pedicatio* 11.

Deprecare camp – 1,10,12,13,14,3,4,5,7,9 – keeps the letter/syllable marking and subject-object order. It yields D P Re C = *deprecare* and the *deprensus/deprecare* echo, *preces dare*. 10 and 3 explicitly note the strict syntactic reading gives deprecare and then note the traditional school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* as the verse-order simplification.

Unresolved nuance remains: whether the author intended the strict syntactic/letter reading *deprecare* with supplication as the poena, which respects the marking and syntax, or the conventional school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicatio* with fettering/stocks, which is the citation tradition. The cumulative round-3 arguments for parallel *sequatur*, the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction, the Pen- vs Pe- problem, and the *deprensus : deprecare* / *dare preces* fit now strongly favour the strict reading *deprecare* = obligation to make supplication/beg pardon as the poena named, while the traditional *pedicare* gloss remains the familiar scholastic/ vulgar form attached to the verse.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The marking the poet gives us is hard to set aside because it is so deliberately asymmetrical.

*Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are all given with *primam/prima* alone. Only Remus is given *syllaba prima Remi*. In charade usage that is the normal way to contrast first element/letter with first syllable. If *primam* were meant as ‘first syllable’ everywhere we would have *syllaba prima Penelopes* just as we have for Remus, and Penelope’s first syllable is *Pen-*, not the truncated *Pe-* the Pe-Di-Ca-Re segmentation needs. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is why the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp keeps slipping between *pedicare* and *pendicare*.

The verb fixes the order in both hemistichs and the construction is parallel.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. *Didonis prima* is the subject made to follow acc. *Penelopes primam*. Let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is the same ellipse: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* is made to follow acc. *primam Cadmi*. Let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.

In the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe we therefore have D after P and Re after C. With *primam/prima* = first letter for Penelope, Dido and Cadmus, P D C, and the only licensed syllable Re- from *syllaba prima Remi*, the composition in the natural subject-object direction is D P Re C.

That is *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’.

The verse then rewards that reading internally. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief is *deprensus* and is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. You *dare preces*; you *deprecare*. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is exactly the kind of pun a school charade sets up, and a guilt that is *luenda* by supplication fits the wording more neatly than a physical fetter.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading also leaves the camp internally split. 11 glosses the form with the later vulgar *pedicatio* sense while 2, 6, 8, 10 gloss the same form with the classical *pedica* ‘foot-fetter, stocks’. Those are not the same penalty, and the split shows the segmentation is being stretched to a familiar word.

Once *primam* is kept as first letter and *sequatur* is kept parallel in both hemistichs, the charade is cleanly D P Re C and the poena the verse names is the obligation to *deprecare*, to give a deprecatio and beg pardon for the theft.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is the same construction with *sequatur*
elided = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi*
is made to follow acc. *primam Cadmi*. Let Remus’ first syllable follow
Cadmus’ first.

In the order the two *sequatur* clauses prescribe we therefore have

*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → D follows P
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re follows C

With *primam/prima* = first letter P, D, C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-,
the composition in the natural subject-object direction of the verbs is

D P Re C = *depreca-*

*quodque fit ex illis* is *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon,
to offer *preces*’.

The closure of the riddle is then the pun it is built on:

*mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

The *fur* who is *deprensus in horto* is told he will *dabis* what is made out
of the pieces, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the poetic way of
saying the guilt is atoned by supplication. You can *dare preces*; *deprecare*
is something you can give. The *deprensus : deprecare* echo is the aesthetic
pay-off of the verse and it makes *dabis* natural.

That is the reading that keeps the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction
intact and respects the subject-object order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs.
The traditional school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f.
‘foot-fetter, stocks, *manica pedis*’, classically *pedicae dare* to fetter/
put in the stocks, later vulgarised as the garden-thief *pedicatio*, is the
verse-order concatenation which flattens *primam* to ‘first syllable’ everywhere,
reverses the second block from Re C to Ca Re and smooths *Pen-* to *Pe-*.
Once the author’s own marking and the parallel *sequatur* construction are
kept consistently the charade is *deprecare* and the poena named for the thief
caught in the *hortus* is the obligation to supplicate, to give a *deprecatio*
and beg pardon.

The two sequatur clauses are doing the work and they are built in parallel.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is written acc. nom. subj. 
Didonis prima is the nom. subject, Penelopes primam the acc. object: 
Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam, ‘let Dido’s first follow
Penelope’s first’. The first block the verb prescribes is therefore P
followed by D, D P in the direction of composition.

The second hemistich is the same construction with sequatur ellipsed:

et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur
primam Cadmi. Nom. syllaba prima Remi is the subject, acc. primam Cadmi
the object: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first. The second
block the verb prescribes is therefore C followed by Re, Re C in the
direction of composition.

The poet marks the material he wants. Syllaba prima is said once and
only for Remus, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. Penelopes primam, Didonis
prima, primam Cadmi are left without syllaba. In Latin charade usage
prima/primam without syllaba is the normal signal for the first
element, the first letter, and syllaba prima is the explicit contrast
for a syllable. If primam were uniformly first syllable we would have
Pen- from Penelope, not Pe-, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain would
already be Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare.

With primam = first letter P D C and syllaba prima Remi = Re-, in the
order imposed by the two sequatur clauses we have

Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam → D P
syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi → Re C

D P Re C = depreca-. Quodque fit ex illis is deprecare/deprecari ‘to
entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’.

That is the reading the verse rewards. mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur,
dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur who is deprensus in horto
is told he will dare what is made out of the pieces, and hac poena culpa
luenda tua est is the poetic way of saying the guilt is atoned by
supplication. Dare preces is exactly what deprecare is, and the
deprensus : deprecare echo is the internal pun on which the charade is
built. The poena named is the obligation to deprecare, to give a
deprecatio and beg pardon for the theft.

The familiar school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare < pedica f. ‘foot-
fetter, stocks, manica pedis’ is the verse-order concatenation which
flattens primam to ‘first syllable’ everywhere, reverses the second
block from Re C to Ca Re and smooths Pen- to Pe-. On that traditional
syllabic verse-order gloss the poena is classically pedicae dare, to be
pedicatus, to be fettered/put in the stocks, the form later vulgarised
in the hortus joke. The strict syntactic/lexical construal which keeps
primam vs syllaba prima distinct and the subject-object order of sequatur
in both hemistichs is D P Re C = deprecare, supplication for pardon.
public_text.10:
The two sequatur clauses are parallel and they are ordinary scholastic charade
instructions.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is in the regular
acc. + nom. + verb order *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* =
*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*.  The nominative is the
follower and the accusative is what is followed: let Dido’s first follow
Penelope’s first. In the order of mention / of composition that is
Penelope’s first then Dido’s first.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* is the same construction with
*sequatur* elided = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. The
nominative *syllaba prima Remi* is the follower and the accusative
*primam Cadmi* is what is followed: let Remus’ first syllable follow
Cadmus’ first. In the order of mention / of composition that is Cadmus’
first then Remus’ first syllable.

The pieces are therefore taken syllabically, as the school charade
tradition does, and the apparent *primam* / *syllaba prima* variation is
the normal metrical variation of the charade.

* Penelopes primam = Pe- : *Pe*-ne-lo-pe
* Didonis prima   = Di- : *Di*-do
* primam Cadmi    = Ca- : *Ca*-d-mus
* Remi syllaba prima = Re- : *Re*-mus

The Pen- vs Pe- objection disappears on correct Latin syllabification.
Penelope is Pe-ne-lo-pe, not Pen-e-lo-pe, so the first syllable is Pe-,
just as Dido is Di-, Cadmus is Ca- and Remus is Re-. The first two
instructions give Pe-Di- and the second two give Ca-Re-.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedica-re* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, manica pedis,
the stocks’.

*pedicare* is *pedicae dare*, to put in the *pedica*, to fetter / shackle
the feet, to put in the stocks. That is what

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena
culpa luenda tua est*

threatens the *fur deprensus in horto* with. The thing made out of Pe-Di-
Ca-Re is the *poena* with which the *culpa* is to be *luenda*: the caught
garden thief is threatened with being *pedicatus*, with being fettered/
put in the stocks, classically *pedicae dare*. In the later vulgar
transmission of the *hortus* joke the same form is the familiar obscene
gloss *pedicatio*.

The *deprensus : deprecare* / *dare preces* play is a very neat rhetorical
reinforcement of the *dabis* of the close and it is the reason the verse is
cited, but it is obtained only by re-analysing *primam* as “first letter”,
by reversing the second *sequatur* from Ca-Re to Re-C and by forcing a
Pen- syllabification for Penelope. Keep the normal school syllabic
reading of *primam/prima* and the subject-object order of the two
parallel *sequatur* clauses and the charade is the traditional
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, the *pedica* / stocks penalty for the thief
caught in the garden.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The grammatical core carried forward is the parallel nominative-accusative construction of *sequatur* and the poet’s own marking of material.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. *Didonis prima* follows acc. *Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The verb therefore fixes a follow-order, not simple verse-order concatenation.

The *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima* distinction is decisive. *Syllaba prima* is said once, only for Remus = Re-. *Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are left without *syllaba*. In Latin charade use *prima/primam* without *syllaba* signals first element / first letter, *syllaba prima* signals an explicit syllable. If *primam* were first syllable throughout Penelope would give *Pen-*, not the needed *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain collapses to *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is repeatedly flagged.

With *primam* = first letter P, D, C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, and the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses, we get
*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → D follows P
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re follows C
D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’.

The verse rewards that reading: *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief who is *deprensus* is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces; *dare preces* = *deprecare*. *Hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is atonement by supplication, and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo is the internal pun.

Round 4 public positions: Colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now argue for the strict syntactic/letter reading D P Re C = *deprecare*, keeping the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking and the parallel subject-object order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs. Colleague 5 notes flips of 3,4,10 in prior rounds toward this reading.

Holdout: Colleague 10 maintains the traditional school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks’. It argues *primam/prima* is normal metrical variation for first syllable, Penelope is *Pe-ne-lo-pe* so first syllable is *Pe-*, not *Pen-*, and the two *sequatur* clauses are read in order of mention rather than subject-object direction. That reading requires flattening the *primam / syllaba prima* contrast, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and smoothing Pen- to Pe-.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp remains internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks, 2,6,8,10,12, and vulgar *pedicatio*, 11. The Deprecare camp is now dominant in the current round, with the strict reading giving a clean charade D P Re C and the neat *deprensus/deprecare* / *dare preces* word-play.

Unresolved nuance that remains: whether the author intended the strict syntactic/letter reading *deprecare* as the intended poena, which respects marking and syntax, or whether the traditional school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicatio* is the historically attested gloss attached to the verse. Cumulative evidence for the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking, the parallel *sequatur* syntax, the Pen- vs Pe- problem, and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo now strongly favours the strict reading *deprecare* = obligation to make supplication/beg pardon as the poena named, while the traditional *pedicare* gloss remains the familiar scholastic/vulgar form cited for the verse.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The charade remains contested but round 4 has tipped the weight strongly toward the strict syntactic/letter-marking deprecare reading, with colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now articulating it.

Deprecare camp core claims:
* Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam: nom. Didonis prima follows acc. Penelopes primam. The verb therefore prescribes P → D and C → Re, i.e. in subject-object direction D P Re C.

If primam were first syllable throughout Penelope would give Pen- not Pe-, collapsing Pe-Di-Ca-Re into Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is taken as evidence the marking is deliberate.

Two competing segmentations persist.

**Deprecare reading – now dominant in round 4**

* With *primam/prima* = first letter P D C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, subject-object order gives D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’.

Core pieces unchanged: verse

et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi,

Primam/syllaba prima crux
* primam/prima without syllaba is argued by 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 to be the Latin charade signal for first element/letter; syllaba prima is the explicit contrast for a real syllable. * 10 defends the traditional school reading by syllabifying Penelope as Pe-ne-lo-pe, so the first syllable is indeed Pe-, and claims prima/syllaba prima variation is normal metrical variation of the charade. On that reading primam = first syllable for all four names.

sequatur order
Parallel construction:
Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam. Nom. Didonis prima is the follower, acc. Penelopes primam is what is followed: let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.
et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi. Nom. syllaba prima Remi follows acc. primam Cadmi: let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.

Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam → D follows P → D P
syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi → Re follows C → Re C
→ D P Re C = depreca-, deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’.

mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is deprensus and is told he will dare what is made out of the pieces. Dare preces is idiomatic for deprecare, and deprensus : deprecare is a clear echo. Hac poena culpa luenda tua est fits atonement by supplication.

Pedicare camp

My current standing
Deprecare parsing is the more internally consistent grammatical reading; it respects the poet’s own primam vs syllaba prima marking, keeps sequatur parallel in both hemistichs, yields D P Re C, and explains the deprensus : deprecare / dare preces pun and hac poena culpa luenda.
Pedicare/pedicatio remains the canonical school citation and historical transmission, Pe-Di-Ca-Re, with the concrete hortus penalty of fettering/stocks and the later vulgar gloss. The conflict is primam meaning first letter vs first syllable, and the direction of composition imposed by sequatur vs verse order.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The riddle *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is contested between a strict syntactic/lexical charade and the traditional verse-order school gloss.

Reading A – verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare / pendicare.
* Penelopes primam = Pe- / Pen-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, taken in linear verse order → Pe-Di-Ca-Re.
* *quodque fit ex illis* → *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’; classically *pedicae dare* = to fetter/put in stocks. Later vulgar transmission = obscene *pedicatio*.
* Support: familiar school charade, *syllaba prima* used to secure Re-, *primam/prima* used syllabically for the others.
* Objections: Pe- vs Pen- instability; *primam* would need to be first syllable for Penelope/Dido but first letter for Cadmus; second hemistich must be reversed from Re C to Ca Re to get Ca-Re; internal split between classical *pedica* stocks and vulgar *pedicatio*; *dabis* less natural for a fetter than for *preces dare*.

Reading B – strict syntax D P Re C = deprecare / deprecari.
* *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. *Didonis prima* follows acc. *Penelopes primam* → D follows P.
* Second hemistich elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi* → Re follows C.
* Poet marks material: *syllaba prima* said once and only for Remus → Re-; *primam/prima* for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus is the normal charade signal for first element/letter → P, D, C.
* Order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses gives D P Re C = *depreca-* → *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer *preces*’.
* Pun *deprensus in horto* : *deprecare* and *dabis* = *preces dare* fits well; *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* = atonement by supplication.
* Support in round 4 from 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9: keeps *primam* vs *syllaba prima* distinction intact, respects parallel *sequatur* construction, avoids Pen- vs Pe- strain, explains *deprensus/deprecare* echo.

Round 4 public positions:
1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now explicitly defend the strict grammatical reading D P Re C = *deprecare*, while acknowledging the traditional school gloss *pedicare* as the verse-order concatenation that flattens the marking. 2,3,4,10 have flipped from earlier syllabic defence to noting the syntactic elegance of *deprecare*. 10 is the remaining holdout for the traditional syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* / *pedica* fetter/stocks, arguing Penelope is Pe-ne-lo-pe so Pe- is correct and *primam/prima* variation is normal metrical variation, and that the *deprensus : deprecare* play is only a rhetorical reinforcement. 11 continues to note the traditional citation is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* with classical *pedica* and later vulgar *pedicatio*.

Unresolved:
* whether *primam/prima* means first letter or first syllable; whether Penelope’s first is Pe- or Pen-;
* whether *sequatur* is to be read as verse-order concatenation or as strict subject-object ordering giving D-P and Re-C;
* whether *dabis* is better satisfied by a physical penalty or by *preces dare*;
* whether intended penalty is literal fettering/stocks, vulgar *pedicatio*, or supplication *deprecari*.

Current weighting is strongly shifting toward the syntactically strict *deprecare* reading because of the poet’s explicit *syllaba prima* marking only for Remus, the parallel *sequatur* construction in both hemistichs, and the internal *deprensus/deprecare* pun with *dare preces*, while retaining the traditional *pedicare* = *pedica* fetter/stocks gloss and its later vulgar development as the historically cited school answer.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The charade hinges on the poet’s marking of the pieces and on the subject-object syntax of the two sequatur clauses.

Marking
* primam / prima without syllaba is used for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus. Only Remus is explicitly syllaba prima Remi = Re-.
* In Latin charade usage this is the normal contrast: prima/primam = first element / first letter, syllaba prima = explicit syllable. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it blocks a uniform “first syllable” reading: Penelopes primam would then be Pen-, not the Pe- needed for the verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain; the Pe- vs Pen- strain is repeatedly flagged.

Sequatur order
* Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam: nom. Didonis prima subject, acc. Penelopes primam object → let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first.
* et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi: nom. syllaba prima Remi subject, acc. primam Cadmi object → let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first.
The two hemistichs are parallel with sequatur elided in the second. In the natural subject-object direction the composition is D P Re C.

With primam/prima = first letter P D C and syllaba prima Remi = Re-, the verb-prescribed order is D P Re C = depreca-, deprecare / deprecari ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer preces’.

Closure evidence
* quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est.
* dare preces is the idiomatic collocation for deprecare, and deprensus : deprecare is the internal pun the verse is built on. A guilt luenda by supplication fits hac poena better than a physical penalty presented as something you ‘give’.

Current round 4 position
* 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 argue the strict grammatical reading: keep primam vs syllaba prima distinct, keep the parallel subject-object sequatur, obtain D P Re C = deprecare/deprecari. The poena is the obligation to make supplication, to give a deprecatio and beg pardon for the theft. Colleagues 5,7 note flips by 3,4,10 toward admitting the strict reading.
* 10 remains a holdout for the traditional school syllabic gloss: Penelope = Pe-, Dido = Di-, Cadmus = Ca-, Remus = Re-, Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare < pedica f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks, manica pedis’. 10 defends this by syllabifying Penelope as Pe-ne-lo-pe, and treats primam/syllaba prima variation as metrical. On that verse-order flattening the poena is classically pedicae dare, to be fettered/put in stocks, later vulgarised as the hortus pedicatio joke.
* 11,2,4,6,8 acknowledge the strict syntactic D P Re C = deprecare reading while also noting the traditional verse-order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare as the familiar citation which requires flattening primam to “first syllable” everywhere, reversing the second block from the Re C required by sequatur to Ca Re, and smoothing Pen- to Pe-.

Unresolved / persisting tension
* Whether the poet intended the letter/syllable contrast and strict sequatur order, or the familiar school syllable chain. The grammatical reading is clean and accounts for the marking and the deprensus/deprecare pun; the traditional reading is the citation tradition and explains the widespread Pe-Di-Ca-Re gloss.
* Within the pedicare camp there is internal split between classical pedica ‘fetter/stocks’ and later vulgar sexual sense; both are developments of the same segmentation.

My synthesis now favours the grammatically faithful deprecare reading as the author’s intended construal, while retaining pedicare < pedica as the traditional verse-order gloss that dominates the citation tradition.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The riddle *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur / et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi, quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* has two competing charade construals.

Deprecare reading. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*; nom. *Didonis prima* follows acc. *Penelopes primam*. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*; nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi*. The poet marks the material asymmetrically: *syllaba prima* is said once and only for Remus = Re-, Penelope, Dido, Cadmus are *primam/prima* alone. In Latin charade idiom *prima/primam* without *syllaba* signals first element/letter, *syllaba prima* the explicit syllable contrast. With *primam/prima* = first letter P D C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, the subject-object order of the two *sequatur* clauses gives D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’. The closure rewards it: *deprensus in horto* fur will *dabis* what is made out of the pieces, *dare preces* = *deprecare*, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* = atonement by supplication, with the *deprensus : deprecare* echo. Defended in round 4 by 1,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 and partially by 11. 5 notes flips by 3,4,10 away from verse-order to strict syntax; 7,8,9 stress the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking and the parallel subject-object *sequatur*.

Pedicare reading. Traditional school charade flattens *primam* to first syllable everywhere and takes verse order. *Penelopes primam* = Pe-, *Didonis prima* = Di-, *primam Cadmi* = Ca-, *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, giving Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, manica pedis, stocks’. *pedicare* = *pedicae dare*, to fetter/put in stocks. Classical gloss = fettering/stocks for the garden thief; later vulgar transmission glosses the same form as *pedicatio*. Defended in round 4 by 10 with the syllabification defence *Penelope = Pe-ne-lo-pe* so first syllable is Pe- and the Pen- vs Pe- objection disappears; 11,2,4,6,8 also present this as the familiar school citation. 11 and 4,12,2 now note both construals: strict syntactic/lexical reading is D P Re C = *deprecare*, verse-order syllabic reading is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

Instabilities and disagreements. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp must reverse the second block from Re C required by *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* to Ca Re, smooth Pen- to Pe-, and flatten *primam* vs *syllaba prima*. The camp is internally split on meaning: 11 presses later vulgar *pedicatio*; 2,6,10,12 press classical *pedica* fetter/stocks. The Deprecare camp’s strength is the marking distinction and the *deprensus/deprecare* pun; its weakness is weight of manuscript/traditional citation for *pedicare*.

Unresolved. Authorial intent for strict Latin syntax and letter/syllable marking giving *deprecare* vs conventional school convention where *sequatur* is read as linear concatenation and *primam* = first syllable giving the cited *pedicare*. The grammatical argument for D P Re C is now dominant in the current round; the traditional citation remains the counterweight.

reflection_text.10:
The grammatical core carried forward is the parallel nominative-accusative construction of *sequatur* and the poet’s own marking of material.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. *Didonis prima* follows acc. *Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. The second hemistich is parallel with *sequatur* elided: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nom. *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi* ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. The verb therefore fixes a follow-order, not simple verse-order concatenation.

The *primam/prima* vs *syllaba prima* distinction is decisive. *Syllaba prima* is said once, only for Remus = Re-. *Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi* are left without *syllaba*. In Latin charade use *prima/primam* without *syllaba* signals first element / first letter, *syllaba prima* signals an explicit syllable. If *primam* were first syllable throughout Penelope would give *Pen-*, not the needed *Pe-*, and the familiar Pe-Di-Ca-Re chain collapses to *Pen-Di-Ca-Re* = *pendicare*. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is repeatedly flagged.

With *primam* = first letter P, D, C and *syllaba prima Remi* = Re-, and the order imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses, we get
*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → D follows P
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re follows C
D P Re C = *depreca-*, *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, to beg pardon, to offer *preces*’.

The verse rewards that reading: *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The thief who is *deprensus* is told he will *dare* what is made out of the pieces; *dare preces* = *deprecare*. *Hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is atonement by supplication, and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo is the internal pun.

Round 4 public positions: Colleagues 1,11,12,13,14,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 now argue for the strict syntactic/letter reading D P Re C = *deprecare*, keeping the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking and the parallel subject-object order of *sequatur* in both hemistichs. Colleague 5 notes flips of 3,4,10 in prior rounds toward this reading.

Holdout: Colleague 10 maintains the traditional school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* < *pedica* f. ‘foot-fetter, stocks’. It argues *primam/prima* is normal metrical variation for first syllable, Penelope is *Pe-ne-lo-pe* so first syllable is *Pe-*, not *Pen-*, and the two *sequatur* clauses are read in order of mention rather than subject-object direction. That reading requires flattening the *primam / syllaba prima* contrast, reversing the second block from Re C to Ca Re, and smoothing Pen- to Pe-.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp remains internally split between classical *pedica* fetter/stocks, 2,6,8,10,12, and vulgar *pedicatio*, 11. The Deprecare camp is now dominant in the current round, with the strict reading giving a clean charade D P Re C and the neat *deprensus/deprecare* / *dare preces* word-play.

Unresolved nuance that remains: whether the author intended the strict syntactic/letter reading *deprecare* as the intended poena, which respects marking and syntax, or whether the traditional school citation Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicatio* is the historically attested gloss attached to the verse. Cumulative evidence for the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* marking, the parallel *sequatur* syntax, the Pen- vs Pe- problem, and the *deprensus : deprecare* echo now strongly favours the strict reading *deprecare* = obligation to make supplication/beg pardon as the poena named, while the traditional *pedicare* gloss remains the familiar scholastic/vulgar form cited for the verse.
reflection_text.12:

Deprecare camp core claims:
* Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam: nom. Didonis prima follows acc. Penelopes primam. Parallel construction in the second hemistich with sequatur elided: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi: nom. syllaba prima Remi follows acc. primam Cadmi. The verb therefore prescribes P → D and C → Re, i.e. in subject-object direction D P Re C.
* Poet marks material asymmetrically: syllaba prima is said once and only for Remus = Re-; primam/prima for Penelope, Dido, Cadmus. In Latin charade usage prima without syllaba signals first element/letter, syllaba prima is the explicit contrast for a syllable. If primam were first syllable throughout Penelope would give Pen- not Pe-, collapsing Pe-Di-Ca-Re into Pen-Di-Ca-Re = pendicare. The Pe- vs Pen- strain is taken as evidence the marking is deliberate.
* With primam = first letter P D C and syllaba prima Remi = Re-, the two sequatur clauses give D P Re C = depreca-, deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, beg pardon, offer preces’. The closure rewards it: quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. Dare preces is idiomatic for deprecare; deprensus : deprecare is the internal pun, and culpa luenda by supplication fits dabis neatly.

Pedicare camp residual:

Internal tensions retained:
* Primam meaning letter vs syllable; deliberate contrast primam vs syllaba prima.
* Sequatur to be read strictly syntactically acc+nom+verb with parallel subject-object order vs poetically “let X follow Y in order of mention”.
* Dabis semantics: deprecare can be given as preces dare; pedicare is suffered.
